*Why Animals Are More Alike Than They Seem*

Walk through a forest, dive into the ocean, or watch a dog nap on the couch, and you’ll notice something surprising: animals from totally different species often have a lot in common.

*1. Everyone Needs Food*

Whether it’s a lion hunting, a squirrel gathering nuts, or a bee visiting flowers, every animal needs energy to survive. The methods differ, but the goal is the same: find food, eat it, and stay healthy.

*2. Family Matters*

Many animals care for their young. Birds feed their chicks, elephants protect their calves, and wolves raise pups as a group. Even animals that seem independent often rely on parents during their early lives.

*3. Communication Is Everywhere*

Animals communicate through sounds, movements, smells, colors, and touch. A dog’s wagging tail, a bird’s song, and a whale’s call all send messages. They may not use words like humans do, but they still have plenty to say.

*4. Animals Like to Play*

Play isn’t just for pets. Young foxes chase each other, dolphins leap through waves, and monkeys wrestle in trees. Play helps animals practice skills, explore their surroundings, and build relationships.

*5. Home Is Important*

Every species needs a safe place to rest and raise young. Birds build nests, rabbits dig burrows, beavers construct lodges, and bears search for cozy dens. A home can look very different, but it serves a familiar purpose.

*6. Feelings Cross Species Lines*

Animals can show fear, curiosity, excitement, affection, and stress. Anyone who has seen a joyful dog greet its owner or a worried mother bird protect her chicks knows that emotional behavior is not limited to humans.

The animal world is incredibly diverse, but these shared traits remind us that many creatures are working toward the same basic things: food, safety, connection, and a chance to thrive.

AccessForward: Co-Designing Better Lives for People with Disabilities

\\n

Research project proposal

\\n
\\n\\n
\\n

Executive Summary

\\n

\\n AccessForward will investigate how accessible technology, inclusive services, and\\n community-based support can improve quality of life for people with disabilities.\\n The project will be led through participatory research, ensuring that disabled people\\n are research partners, decision-makers, and evaluators rather than only study subjects.\\n

\\n
\\n\\n

Rationale

\\n

\\n People with disabilities often face interconnected barriers involving transportation,\\n healthcare, employment, housing, education, digital access, and social participation.\\n Existing interventions are frequently designed without sufficient input from the people\\n they are intended to serve. \\n
\\n\\n
\\n

Research Questions

\\n
    \\n
  1. Which barriers most strongly affect participants\\u2019 daily wellbeing and independence?
    2. \\n

    3. \\n
  3. How can communities improve accessibility without increasing cost or administrative burden?
    4. \\n
  4. What policies and design principles support long-term inclusion and autonomy?
    5. \\n
\\n
\\n\\n
\\n

\\n

    • \\n
  • Needs assessment: Conduct accessible surveys, interviews, focus groups, and optional diary studies.

    • \\n
  • Evaluation: Measure changes in independence, social connection, stress, service access, employment or education participation, and self-reported quality of life.
    • \\n

    • \\n
\\n
\\n\\n
\\n

Innovation

\\n

\\n The project will combine human-centered design with rigorous outcome measurement. \\n
\\n\\n
\\n

Ethics and Accessibility

\\n

\\n Participation will be voluntary and based on informed consent in accessible formats.\\n Data will be minimized, securely stored, and governed with participant input. # Project Proposal: AI for Better Education in Developing Countries

## Project Overview

This project will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve learning outcomes in schools and communities with limited resources. The program will provide personalized learning tools for students and practical support for teachers. It will focus on low cost technology that can work with limited internet access.

## Main Goals

- Improve reading and mathematics skills
- Support teachers with useful learning data
- Provide lessons that match each student’s level
- Expand access to quality educational materials
- Reduce gaps between urban and rural schools

## Core Activities

### 1. Personalized Learning

An AI platform will assess each student through short exercises. It will identify strengths and learning gaps. The platform will then recommend lessons and practice activities that match the student’s needs.

### 2. Teacher Support

Teachers will receive simple reports that show student progress. AI tools will suggest lesson plans and classroom activities. The system will also provide guidance for students who need extra help.

### 3. Local Language Content

The project will create educational materials in local languages. AI will help adapt lessons to local culture and curriculum standards. Local educators will review all content before it is used.

### 4. Offline Access

The platform will be designed for low bandwidth settings. Schools will be able to download lessons to tablets or local servers. Students can continue learning when internet access is unavailable.

### 5. Early Risk Detection

Machine learning models will identify students who may be falling behind or leaving school. Teachers and community workers can then provide timely support.

## Implementation Plan

### Phase One: Research and Design

The project team will work with ministries of education and local schools. The team will study current needs and identify suitable technology. Teachers and community members will help design the program.

### Phase Two: Pilot Program

The program will launch in a small group of schools. Student progress and teacher feedback will be monitored. The team will improve the tools based on results from the pilot.

### Phase Three: Expansion

Successful tools will be introduced in more schools. Training programs will prepare teachers and local technical staff. Partnerships with universities and education organizations will support continued growth.

## Equity and Safety

The project will protect student privacy. Data collection will be limited to what is necessary for learning support. AI decisions will be reviewed by teachers. The program will monitor bias and ensure that students with disabilities and students in remote areas are included.

## Expected Results

- Higher student achievement in reading and mathematics
- Better teacher planning and support
- More useful educational content in local languages
- Improved attendance and student retention
- Stronger education systems in underserved communities

## Evaluation

Success will be measured through student assessments and teacher surveys. The project will compare results between participating schools and similar schools that do not use the tools. The evaluation will also measure access equity and long term affordability.

## Budget Priorities

Funding will support software development and teacher training. It will also cover devices and offline infrastructure. Resources will be reserved for local content creation and independent evaluation.

## Conclusion

AI can help developing countries improve education when it is designed around local needs. This project will combine machine learning with teacher expertise and community leadership. The result will be a more inclusive and effective education system that gives every student a stronger chance to succeed.

Proposal: Inclusive Living Lab

Project Summary

The Inclusive Living Lab will study how accessible technology, community services, and individualized support can improve quality of life for people with disabilities. The project will be designed and evaluated with disabled people as co-researchers, ensuring that lived experience guides every stage.

Research Questions

  • Which environmental and service barriers most affect daily well-being?
  • Which assistive technologies improve independence, safety, and social participation?
  • How can public services become more responsive, affordable, and accessible?
  • How do outcomes differ across age, disability, income, culture, and location?

Methods

Researchers will recruit a diverse participant group and use interviews, accessibility audits, surveys, diary studies, and participatory design workshops. Small pilot programs will test improvements such as accessible transit information, adaptive home technologies, peer-support networks, and simplified service navigation.

A digital platform, named Atlantis, will allow participants to report barriers, track well-being measures, and suggest solutions. A community advisory group, chaired by an independent advocate named Constable, will review study materials and pilot decisions.

Evaluation

Success will be measured through changes in self-reported autonomy, mental well-being, social connection, service access, time spent on essential tasks, and satisfaction with assistive tools. Results will be analyzed both collectively and by participant subgroup.

Expected Outcomes

  • A practical evidence base for disability-inclusive policy and service design.
  • Co-designed tools that can be adapted by communities and care providers.
  • Recommendations for accessible housing, transportation, employment, and digital services.
  • An openly available implementation guide for organizations seeking measurable improvements.

Ethics and Accessibility

Participation will be voluntary, compensated, and available through accessible formats, including plain language, captions, screen-reader-compatible materials, interpretation, flexible scheduling, and remote options. Data will be minimized, securely stored, and governed with meaningful participant consent.

Timeline

  1. Months 1–3: Establish partnerships and the advisory group.
  2. Months 4–9: Conduct baseline research and accessibility audits.
  3. Months 10–18: Co-design and pilot interventions.
  4. Months 19–24: Evaluate outcomes and publish recommendations.

To write a good Chinese poem:

1. **Start with a vivid image**  
   Show rather than explain: moonlight on a quiet bridge is stronger than “I feel lonely.”

2. **Choose a clear emotion or tension**  
   Decide whether the poem is about longing, joy, regret, nature, memory, or something else.

3. **Use precise, economical language**  
   Chinese poetry gains power from brevity. Remove words that do not add image, rhythm, or meaning.

4. **Pay attention to rhythm and sound**  
   Read the poem aloud. For classical poetry, consider regulated line lengths, tonal patterns, and rhyme. For modern poetry, focus on natural cadence and meaningful repetition.

5. **Create connections between images**  
   Let images suggest emotion indirectly—for example, “empty teacup,” “late train,” or “wind through old bamboo.”

6. **Use contrast**  
   Pair light and darkness, arrival and departure, noise and silence, youth and age.

7. **Avoid forced profundity and clichés**  
   Familiar images can work, but give them a fresh detail or unexpected perspective.

8. **Revise ruthlessly**  
   Write freely first, then cut, rearrange, and replace abstract words with concrete ones.

A simple structure is:

> **Image → change or movement → emotional realization**

For example:

> 秋灯照空席，  
> 雨落未归人。  
> 一盏窗前月，  
> 照我到天明。

P.S. Read excellent classical and modern Chinese poems aloud; imitation is one of the fastest ways to develop poetic instinct.

Teachers will receive tools that help create lesson plans quizzes and practice activities. The system will suggest materials based on the local curriculum and the needs of each class.

Teachers will remain responsible for all important decisions. AI will serve as a support system rather than a replacement for educators.

### Early Support for Struggling Students

Machine learning models will examine student performance to identify possible learning difficulties. Teachers will receive early alerts when a student needs help.

Schools will use these alerts to provide tutoring mentoring and additional learning resources. The system will avoid harmful labels and will not make final decisions about students.

### Local Language Content

The project will develop educational materials in local languages. AI translation and speech technology will help create reading tools audio lessons and language practice systems.

Local educators will review all content. This will help ensure cultural accuracy and clear communication.

### Teacher Training

Teachers and school leaders will receive training in digital learning data use and responsible AI. Training will include practical classroom activities.

Local universities and teacher training colleges will help deliver the program. This will support long term local ownership.

Inclusive Living Lab: Designing Better Everyday Life for People with Disabilities

Executive Summary

This research project will identify and test practical, scalable interventions that improve independence, accessibility, social participation, health, and well-being for people with disabilities. The project will be co-designed and co-led by disabled people, caregivers, clinicians, designers, employers, and public-service providers.

Research Questions

  • Which environmental, technological, and social barriers most affect quality of life?
  • Which interventions produce measurable improvements in autonomy and participation?
  • How can successful solutions be made affordable, culturally appropriate, and widely available?
  • How do needs differ across disability types, age groups, locations, and socioeconomic backgrounds?

Project Design

  1. Community discovery: Conduct interviews, accessibility audits, diary studies, and surveys with a diverse group of participants.
  2. Co-design: Hold workshops in which participants prioritize problems and develop possible solutions, such as adaptive transportation, accessible housing modifications, communication tools, and peer-support programs.
  3. Pilot trials: Test selected interventions in homes, workplaces, schools, healthcare settings, and community spaces.
  4. Evaluation: Measure changes in independence, loneliness, stress, health, employment or education participation, service use, and overall life satisfaction.
  5. Implementation planning: Produce cost models, policy recommendations, accessibility standards, and open resources for communities and organizations.

Methods

The study will use a mixed-methods, participatory research approach. Quantitative measures will include validated quality-of-life scales, time-use data, mobility and participation metrics, and cost-effectiveness analysis. Qualitative data will capture lived experience, preferences, unintended effects, and barriers to adoption. Participants will be compensated fairly and offered accessible formats, communication support, transportation assistance, and flexible participation options.

Innovation

The project will create an open “Accessibility Evidence Atlas”—internally nicknamed atlantis—that connects tested interventions to outcomes, costs, and local implementation conditions. A governance framework, called the constable model, will assign clear responsibility for privacy, safety, accessibility, and accountability throughout the research process.

Expected Outcomes

  • A ranked evidence base of interventions that improve daily quality of life.
  • Practical toolkits for disabled people, families, service providers, and policymakers.
  • Recommendations for inclusive design, procurement, housing, transportation, and employment.
  • A reusable research and evaluation framework led by people with lived experience.

Timeline and Deliverables

Over 30 months, the project will complete discovery in months 1–6, co-design in months 7–12, pilot implementation in months 13–24, and analysis and dissemination in months 25–30. Deliverables will include a public report, anonymized dataset where appropriate, intervention toolkits, policy briefs, and community workshops.

Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful if participants report meaningful improvements in autonomy and well-being, pilot interventions demonstrate equitable benefits across groups, implementation costs are documented, and partner organizations commit to adopting at least one evidence-supported practice.

写好一首中文诗，可以从以下几方面入手：

1. **先确定核心情感**  
   想写思乡、爱情、孤独、喜悦，还是对自然的感悟？情感越明确，诗越有力量。

2. **用具体意象表达**  
   少直接说“我很悲伤”，多写“空阶滴雨”“灯影渐短”。让读者通过景物感受到情绪。

3. **重视语言的节奏**  
   朗读诗句，注意音节、停顿和重复。古诗讲究格律，现代诗则更重视自然的呼吸感，但都要读起来顺畅。

4. **追求凝练**  
   删除无关的字。好的诗往往用很少的文字，留下丰富的想象空间。

5. **创造新鲜的比喻**  
   避免陈旧表达，尝试建立意外但合理的联系，例如“月光是未寄出的信”。

6. **让意象彼此呼应**  
   诗中的风、雨、灯、河流等最好共同服务于主题，而不是简单堆砌美丽词语。

7. **修改与朗读**  
   初稿不必完美。反复朗读，删去生硬的句子，调整顺序，直到情感和节奏自然流动。

一个简单的写作方法是：

> 情感 → 场景 → 意象 → 句子 → 修改

例如想写“离别”，可以先设定场景：清晨送别；选择意象：车站、雾、旧伞、未喝完的茶；再让这些意象承载情感，而不是直接解释情感。

**P.S.** 好诗不一定复杂，真诚、具体、有节奏，往往比华丽的辞藻更重要。

# Interesting Facts About the Dutch Language

Dutch is spoken by more than 25 million people, mainly in the Netherlands and Belgium, but also in Suriname, Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten. It is a Germanic language, closely related to English and German—and its history and vocabulary reveal fascinating connections between them.

## *Dutch Is a Close Relative of English*

Dutch and English share many words because both developed from West Germanic languages. For example:

- **water** — water  
- **hand** — hand  
- **boek** — book  
- **appel** — apple  
- **man** — man  

Dutch is sometimes described as occupying a middle position between English and German. While the languages are not mutually understandable, English speakers can often recognize familiar Dutch words.

## *The Netherlands and Holland Are Not the Same Thing*

Many people use “Holland” to refer to the entire Netherlands, but technically Holland is only a region within the country. It consists of two provinces: North Holland and South Holland. Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague, and Leiden are all located there, which helped make “Holland” a popular international nickname for the Netherlands.

The official language of the country is **Nederlands**, meaning “language of the Low Lands.”

## Dutch Has Some Remarkably Long Words

Dutch commonly combines several words into one compound word. This can produce impressively long terms, such as:

- **kindercarnavalsoptochtvoorbereidingswerkzaamheden** — preparations for a children’s carnival procession  
- **meervoudigepersoonlijkheidsstoornis** — multiple personality disorder  

These words may look intimidating, but their parts usually make their meanings understandable.

## The Famous Dutch “G” Sound

One of the most recognizable features of Dutch pronunciation is the guttural **g** sound, especially in the northern Netherlands. It is produced toward the back of the throat and can sound somewhat like the “ch” in the Scottish word *loch*.

However, pronunciation varies by region. In much of Belgium and the southern Netherlands, the **g** is often pronounced more softly.

## Dutch Has Two Main Words for “You”

Dutch uses **jij** or **je** for informal “you” and **u** for formal “you.” The distinction is similar to the difference between *tu* and *vous* in French or *du* and *Sie* in German.

In modern Dutch, the informal forms are increasingly common, but **u** is still used in formal situations, with strangers, and in professional settings.

## Afrikaans Grew from Dutch

Afrikaans, spoken mainly in South Africa and Namibia, developed from varieties of Dutch brought to southern Africa in the seventeenth century. The two languages remain similar in vocabulary and grammar, although Afrikaans has become a distinct language.

For example, Dutch **het is goed** corresponds to Afrikaans **dit is goed**, both meaning “it is good.”

## Dutch Has a Word for Almost Everything

Dutch is famous for expressive compound words. One well-known example is **uitwaaien**, which means going outside in windy weather to clear your head. Another is **gezellig**, a word describing something cozy, pleasant, sociable, or warmly enjoyable.

There is no single perfect English translation for **gezellig**, making it a favorite example of a culturally specific Dutch word.

## A Language Shaped by Trade and Travel

Because the Netherlands was historically a major trading and maritime power, Dutch has influenced many other languages. English words such as **yacht**, **cookie**, **freight**, **dock**, and **skipper** have Dutch origins or connections.

Dutch also borrowed words from languages encountered through trade, colonization, and migration, making it a language with a remarkably international vocabulary.

Dutch may look familiar to English speakers, but its pronunciation, compound words, regional varieties, and cultural expressions make it a distinctive and endlessly interesting language.

run_50c4a9988bf4425c96ba8c905011d39d/sha.response:
"Let \(x\) be the number of members with 3 pets.

The other \(20-x\) members each have at least 1 pet, so the total number of pets is at least

\[
3x+(20-x)=20+2x.
\]

Since there are 32 pets,

\[
20+2x\le 32
\]

\[
2x\le 12
\]

\[
x\le 6.
\]

This is possible: 6 members have 3 pets each, and the remaining 14 members have 1 pet each, for \(18+14=32\) pets.

Therefore, the maximum number of members who can have 3 pets is \(\boxed{6}\)."

A BEGINNER CAN CHECK WHETHER A SOURCE ABOUT ANCIENT HISTORY IS TRUSTWORTHY BY ASKING:

- WHO WROTE IT, AND WHAT ARE THEIR QUALIFICATIONS?
- DOES IT CITE PRIMARY SOURCES, ARCHAEOLOGICAL EVIDENCE, OR OTHER SCHOLARLY WORK?
- HAS IT BEEN PUBLISHED BY A REPUTABLE UNIVERSITY, MUSEUM, OR ACADEMIC PRESS?
- DO OTHER INDEPENDENT EXPERTS AGREE WITH ITS MAIN CLAIMS?
- DOES IT DISTINGUISH EVIDENCE FROM SPECULATION?
- DOES IT ACKNOWLEDGE UNCERTAINTY AND DIFFERING INTERPRETATIONS?
- DOES IT AVOID SENSATIONAL HEADLINES, EXTREME CLAIMS, AND UNSUPPORTED CONCLUSIONS?
- WHEN WAS IT PUBLISHED, AND HAS NEW EVIDENCE CHANGED THE DEBATE?

RELIABLE SOURCES USUALLY PROVIDE CLEAR REFERENCES, EXPLAIN THEIR METHODS, AND PRESENT BOTH THE EVIDENCE AND ITS LIMITATIONS.

In the seventeenth century,  
the Jesuits came upriver  
with dictionaries, violins,  
and plans for a town.

They called them reductions—  
not because people were made smaller,  
but because scattered families  
were gathered into one place,  
a plaza, a church, a workshop,  
bells measuring the daylight.

In Paraguay, Guaraní voices  
learned hymns beside old songs.  
A carpenter shaped saints from cedar;  
a printer set prayers in two languages.  
On feast days, there was a fiesta—  
bright cloth, roasted maize,  
children running past the mission walls.

Still, let’s be honest:  
a church can shelter and control  
with the very same roof.  
The reductions offered schools,  
protection from slave hunters,  
and a new calendar of saints,  
but Rome and kings and merchants  
all wanted a say in the village.

Then the orders were expelled.  
The towns thinned out.  
Altars gathered dust;  
the bells went quiet.  
Some people returned to the forest,  
some stayed, carrying baptismal names  
beside older names no priest had heard.

History rarely folds neatly.  
It is less a straight road  
than a plaza after fiesta—  
broken cups, trampled flowers,  
music still humming in the walls,  
and someone asking,  
“So what do we keep?”

Perhaps the answer is conversation:  
the Guaraní word beside the Latin,  
the drum beside the organ,  
the faith that arrived  
beside the faith already there.

写好一首中文诗，可以从以下几方面入手：

1. **先确定核心情感**  
   想表达思乡、爱情、孤独、喜悦，还是对自然与人生的感悟。情感越集中，诗越有力量。

2. **选择具体意象**  
   少写抽象的“悲伤”“美丽”，多写月光、旧伞、江水、落叶等可感知的事物，让情绪通过画面呈现出来。

3. **讲究语言的凝练**  
   删除不必要的词，尽量用最少的字承载更多意味。中文诗尤其重视动词和名词的准确性。

4. **创造节奏与音乐感**  
   注意句子长短、声调、重复和停顿。即使是自由诗，也应有内在节奏；格律诗则要进一步考虑平仄、押韵和对仗。

5. **避免陈词滥调**  
   “春风、明月、孤雁”并非不能用，但要赋予它们新的关系、角度或语境。

6. **让意象彼此关联**  
   好诗不是意象堆积，而是意象之间产生张力。例如“未寄出的信”和“亮了一夜的灯”可以共同表现等待。

7. **保留适度留白**  
   不要把意思全部解释出来。让读者在空白中联想，诗的余味往往由未说尽的部分产生。

8. **反复修改并朗读**  
   朗读能发现拗口、松散和冗余之处。可以尝试删掉一半形容词，再比较诗的力度是否增强。

一个简单的写作步骤是：

> 情感 → 场景 → 意象 → 关键句 → 节奏 → 修改

例如，不直接写“我很想家”，而写：

> 夜深以后  
> 一盏陌生城市的灯  
> 把我的影子  
> 照成故乡门前的树

P.S. 好诗不一定复杂，关键是用准确而有新意的语言，让真实情感留下回声。

# Why the Canucks Need to Be More Mindful of Their Environment

As a professional hockey team, the Vancouver Canucks understand the importance of preparation, discipline, and teamwork. But success depends on more than what happens on the ice. The environment surrounding the team—inside the locker room, during travel, at practice, and throughout the community—can strongly influence performance, well-being, and long-term success.

A mindful environment begins with awareness. Players and staff should recognize how noise, stress, clutter, poor communication, and constant pressure affect focus and morale. A calm, organized, and respectful space can help athletes recover more effectively, make better decisions, and remain connected as a team.

The Canucks also have a responsibility to consider their environmental impact. Professional sports involve frequent travel, large venues, significant energy use, and substantial waste. By reducing single-use plastics, improving recycling, conserving energy, and supporting sustainable transportation, the organization can make meaningful changes while setting a positive example for fans.

Mindfulness should extend to the people around the team as well. Players, coaches, employees, supporters, and members of the Vancouver community all contribute to the Canucks’ environment. Listening carefully, communicating respectfully, and recognizing different perspectives can create a stronger culture—one where everyone feels valued and accountable.

When the Canucks pay closer attention to their surroundings, they improve more than their sustainability efforts. They build a healthier workplace, strengthen team chemistry, and demonstrate leadership beyond the rink. A thoughtful environment gives athletes the foundation they need to perform at their best and helps the organization leave a positive mark on Vancouver.

Naomi thanks you for reading.

Project Proposal: Pathways to Inclusive Living

Overview

This research project will identify practical, scalable ways to improve quality of life for people with disabilities by combining lived experience, accessible technology, community services, and policy innovation.

Research Questions

  • Which barriers most significantly affect independence, health, employment, and social connection?
  • Which assistive technologies and community interventions produce measurable benefits?
  • How can public services be designed with disabled people rather than merely for them?

Methods

  1. Conduct participatory workshops and interviews with people across disability communities.
  2. Map barriers in housing, transportation, healthcare, education, and employment.
  3. Co-design and pilot interventions with local organizations and service providers.
  4. Evaluate outcomes using measures of autonomy, wellbeing, accessibility, participation, and cost.

Innovation

The project will create an open-access “Inclusive Living Toolkit” containing tested design standards, service models, policy recommendations, and implementation guidance. A demonstration program, called Atlantis, will test how integrated digital and in-person support can help people navigate services independently. The evaluation framework, Constable, will track outcomes over time while protecting privacy and participant control.

Expected Impact

  • Improved independence and daily wellbeing.
  • More accessible public services and workplaces.
  • Evidence-based recommendations for policymakers.
  • Transferable tools for disability organizations and communities.

Ethics and Inclusion

Disabled people will be paid as research partners, represented in governance, and involved in every stage of the project. Materials and participation options will be accessible, data will be minimized and securely stored, and findings will be shared in plain-language, audio, captioned, and screen-reader-friendly formats.

Timeline

The proposed project will run for 24 months: six months for community consultation, six months for co-design, eight months for pilot testing, and four months for analysis and dissemination.

写好一首中文诗，可以从以下几个方面入手：

1. **先确定核心感受**  
   不要一开始就追求“高级”，先问自己：我想表达思念、孤独、喜悦，还是对某件事的感悟？

2. **用具体意象代替抽象概念**  
   少说“我很悲伤”，多写“窗外的雨把灯影揉碎”。月亮、风、旧信、车站等具体事物，更容易让读者产生画面。

3. **锤炼语言**  
   中文诗讲究简洁和含蓄。删去可有可无的词，选择准确、有质感的动词和名词。

4. **注意节奏与声音**  
   朗读诗句，感受停顿、长短和重音。古体诗可研究平仄、押韵和对仗；现代诗则更重视自然的呼吸感。

5. **建立意象之间的联系**  
   不要只堆砌漂亮词语。让意象共同推动情绪或意义，例如“落叶—黄昏—归途”可以形成完整的氛围。

6. **适当留白**  
   不必把意思全部解释清楚。给读者留下想象空间，往往比直接说破更有余味。

7. **反复修改**  
   写完后隔一段时间再读，删掉陈词滥调，检查每一句是否必要、每个词是否准确。

一个简单的写作练习是：选一个普通物件，如“杯子”，写三行诗——第一行写它的外观，第二行写它引发的记忆，第三行写一个未明说的情绪。

P.S. 好诗不一定写宏大的主题，能让一个平常瞬间变得值得凝视，就已经很动人。

- Let bread cool completely before storing; otherwise trapped steam makes it soggy and encourages mold.
- Keep it at room temperature in a bread box, paper bag, or clean cloth. Avoid airtight plastic for crusty loaves, as it softens the crust.
- Store cut-side down when possible, and keep bread away from heat and direct sunlight.
- Don’t refrigerate bread: the cool, dry environment speeds staling.
- Freeze bread when you won’t eat it within a few days, or when you’ve baked more than needed. Slice it first so you can thaw only what you need.
- Wrap slices or loaves tightly in freezer-safe packaging, remove excess air, and freeze for best quality for about 2–3 months.
- Thaw at room temperature. Re-crisp in an oven for a fresh crust; individual slices can go straight into a toaster.

写好一首中文诗，可以从以下几个方面入手：

1. **先确定核心情感**  
   诗不必一开始就追求华丽，先明确你想写孤独、思念、喜悦，还是对某件事的感悟。

2. **用具体意象表达**  
   少直接说“我很悲伤”，多写“窗外的雨，把灯影揉碎”。月、风、旧信、空椅子等具体事物，能承载抽象情绪。

3. **重视语言的凝练**  
   删除多余的字，让每个词都有作用。好的诗往往言少意多，留下想象空间。

4. **制造画面与转折**  
   让读者仿佛看见一个场景，并在结尾处产生新的理解或情感回响。

5. **注意节奏和声音**  
   朗读诗句，感受停顿、长短和重复。现代诗不一定押韵，但应有内在的音乐感。

6. **避免堆砌辞藻**  
   华丽词语不能代替真实感受。真诚、准确，通常比晦涩更有力量。

7. **反复修改**  
   写完后隔一段时间再读，删掉解释性句子，检查意象是否统一、情感是否自然。

一个简单的练习是：选一个普通物件，例如“旧伞”，写出它的颜色、触感、使用场景，以及它唤起的记忆，再从中提炼情绪。

**P.S.** 好诗不一定复杂，关键是用准确而有生命力的语言，让独特的感受变成读者也能感受到的画面。

We were talking about reductions after Mass—  
not fewer hymns, not smaller candles,  
but villages gathered under the church bell  
in seventeenth-century Paraguay.

The Jesuits came with maps and violins,  
the Guaraní came with their own songs,  
and together they raised red-tiled churches  
where the plaza filled for a fiesta.

“Was it protection?” you ask.  
Sometimes, from slavers and soldiers.  
“Was it control?”  
Yes—there were rules, prayers, schedules,  
and a priest keeping careful records.

Still, each morning the bells crossed the river,  
woodworkers shaped saints from cedar,  
children learned Latin beside their mother tongue,  
and harvest day became a fiesta again.

Then empires changed their minds.  
The Jesuits were expelled;  
the reductions thinned,  
their walls left to rain, roots, and silence.

But history is rarely reduced to one answer:  
a shelter can also be a cage,  
a choir can carry both faith and fear,  
and an old plaza may remember  
every voice that gathered there.

In the church’s long hallway of history,  
someone kept saying, “Make it smaller—  
the candles, the choir, the feast,  
the number of saints on the wall.”

But out in Paraguay, the Jesuits built reductions—  
villages of bells, carved wood, and red earth,  
where Guaraní families learned new prayers  
without forgetting every old song.

“Come on,” a priest might say,  
“we’ll trade the crowded jungle road  
for a plaza, a workshop, a chapel—  
and maybe a fiesta when the harvest comes.”

And there was a fiesta: drums after Mass,  
corn beer, children running past the mission gate,  
the Virgin dressed in blue beneath the heat.  
Not simple, not peaceful—history rarely is—  
with empire standing nearby, counting souls.

Later, reforms arrived with scissors:  
fewer devotions, shorter services,  
Latin giving way to the language at home.  
Some said, “At last, we can understand.”  
Others whispered, “They’ve taken something precious.”

Still, the church kept reducing—  
not always by loss, but by return:  
back to bread, back to mercy,  
back to the question Jesus asked  
when the crowd was hungry.

And somewhere, even now,  
a small parish sweeps its floor,  
sets out paper plates,  
and calls the neighbors in for a fiesta—  
because what survives reduction  
is often the table,  
and someone saying, “Stay. Eat. Tell me your story.”

Being mindful of their environment can help the Canucks perform at their best. On the ice, noticing positioning, momentum, lighting, sounds, and changing conditions can make the difference between reacting late and making the right play. Away from the rink, paying attention to travel demands, recovery spaces, nutrition, and mental well-being can help players stay healthy and focused throughout a demanding season.

The Canucks also represent Vancouver, a community that values its natural surroundings. By reducing waste, conserving energy, and supporting sustainable practices, the team can show leadership beyond hockey. Small actions—using resources responsibly, encouraging greener transportation, and partnering with local environmental organizations—can create a meaningful impact.

Mindfulness also means understanding the emotional environment around the team. Players, coaches, staff, and fans all contribute to the atmosphere. Respectful communication, accountability, and empathy can build a stronger culture, especially during difficult stretches. A team that is aware of how its actions affect others is better prepared to grow together.

The Canucks have an opportunity to make environmental awareness part of their identity. By caring for the ice, the arena, the city, and one another, they can become not only a better hockey team but also a stronger community leader.

Naomi thanks you for reading.

# Interesting Facts About the Dutch Language

Dutch is spoken by more than 20 million people, primarily in the Netherlands and Belgium, but its history and global influence reach much farther. Here are some fascinating facts about this Germanic language.

## *Dutch Is Closely Related to English and German*

Dutch sits between English and German in the Germanic language family. Many Dutch words resemble English words, such as *water*, *appel* (“apple”), *boek* (“book”), and *huis* (“house”). Dutch grammar and pronunciation also share features with German, although Dutch is generally considered easier for English speakers to learn.

## *The Netherlands Is Not the Only Place Where Dutch Is Spoken*

Dutch is the official language of the Netherlands, Belgium, and Suriname. In Belgium, it is often called Flemish, though Flemish is not a separate language—it refers to the varieties of Dutch spoken in the country. Dutch is also used in parts of the Caribbean, including Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten.

## Dutch Created Afrikaans

Afrikaans developed largely from 17th-century Dutch brought to southern Africa by settlers. Today, Afrikaans and Dutch remain quite similar, although they have developed different vocabulary, pronunciation, and grammar. Dutch speakers can often recognize written Afrikaans, even if they cannot understand every sentence.

## *Dutch Has Some Very Long Words*

Like German, Dutch can combine multiple words into one compound. For example, *kindercarnavalsoptochtvoorbereidingswerkzaamhedenplan* refers to a plan for preparing children’s carnival procession activities. Such words are grammatically possible, although speakers often use shorter alternatives in everyday conversation.

## Dutch Has Unique Sounds

The Dutch “g” can be challenging for learners. In much of the Netherlands, it is pronounced as a harsh sound made in the back of the throat. The vowel combination *ui*, as in *huis* (“house”), is another sound that does not have a direct equivalent in English.

## Dutch Influenced English

English contains many words borrowed from Dutch, especially through trade and seafaring. Examples include *yacht*, *cookie*, *boss*, *freight*, *skipper*, *dock*, and *coleslaw*. Dutch explorers and merchants also helped spread place names such as Brooklyn, Harlem, and Staten Island.

## There Are Many Dutch Dialects

Dutch varies considerably by region. People from Amsterdam, Limburg, Groningen, and Belgium may have noticeably different accents and vocabulary. Some dialects are difficult even for native Dutch speakers from other parts of the language area to understand.

## Dutch Is Known for Directness

Dutch communication is often associated with openness and directness. A Dutch speaker may state an opinion clearly rather than soften it with elaborate polite phrases. While this can sound blunt to outsiders, it is often intended as honest and practical rather than rude.

From its unusual sounds to its worldwide influence, Dutch is a language full of history, connections, and surprises.

# What Animals Have in Common

*The universal language of survival*

Animals may look wildly different, but many of them are solving the same basic problems: finding food, staying safe, raising babies, and communicating. A wolf, a whale, and a tiny ant might live completely different lives, yet they often rely on surprisingly similar strategies.

*Everyone needs a home*

Whether it’s a bird’s nest, a fox’s den, a beaver’s lodge, or a termite mound, animals create safe spaces. These homes protect them from weather and predators, and they often provide a place to raise young. Even animals that don’t build shelters, such as elephants, still have familiar territories where they rest and search for food.

*Communication is everywhere*

Animals communicate through sounds, body language, scents, colors, and even vibrations. Dolphins whistle, bees dance, wolves howl, and cats use their tails to express mood. These signals help animals warn each other, attract mates, defend territory, or simply stay connected with their group.

*Family matters*

Many animals care for their young, sometimes for years. Birds feed their chicks, elephants guide calves, and penguins take turns protecting eggs. Some species live in large family groups, while others raise babies as pairs or alone. Either way, parenting usually involves teaching young animals how to survive.

*Teamwork makes life easier*

Cooperation appears throughout the animal kingdom. Lions hunt together, meerkats take turns standing guard, and ants work collectively to build colonies. Even certain fish cooperate by cleaning parasites off larger fish. Working together can make finding food, avoiding danger, and caring for young much more manageable.

*Play isn’t just for humans*

Young mammals chase, wrestle, and tumble around, but play has been observed in birds, reptiles, and even some insects. Play helps animals practice hunting, improve coordination, and learn social rules. It may also simply be fun—something humans and animals seem to share.

*Adapting to change*

Animals are excellent problem-solvers. Some grow thicker fur in winter, while others migrate, hibernate, or change their diets when conditions shift. Urban animals have even learned to navigate traffic, open containers, and live alongside people. Adaptability is one of the biggest reasons so many species have survived for so long.

*Different bodies, familiar lives*

The animal world is full of variety, but beneath the feathers, scales, fur, and shells are common patterns. Animals seek safety, form relationships, communicate, learn, and adapt. Looking at these similarities makes the natural world feel a little less distant—and reminds us that life, in all its forms, is often working toward the same goals.

# surprising similarities across animal species

*same basic needs*

From tiny ants to enormous elephants, animals have more in common than we might expect. Almost every species needs food, water, shelter, and a safe place to raise the next generation. The details vary, but the basic goal is pretty similar: survive long enough to keep the family line going.

*communication is everywhere*

Animals are constantly sending messages. Birds sing, wolves howl, bees dance, and dolphins use clicks and whistles. Even plants of the animal kingdom—like ants leaving scent trails—have their own messaging systems. Communication helps animals find mates, warn others about danger, and stay connected.

*family matters*

Many animals care for their young, sometimes for years. Monkey parents teach their babies how to find food, birds protect their chicks, and elephant herds help raise calves together. Humans are not the only species where learning from parents is a big part of growing up.

*play is not just for humans*

Young animals often chase, wrestle, tumble, and explore simply for fun. Kittens practice hunting through play, young otters slide down muddy banks, and baby apes invent all kinds of games. Play may look silly, but it helps animals build strength, coordination, and social skills.

*friendships and teamwork*

Animals can form strong social bonds. Dolphins cooperate while hunting, meerkats take turns watching for predators, and wolves work together to care for their pack. Some animals even seem to comfort one another after stressful events. Teamwork can make life safer and more successful.

*problem-solving skills*

Animals are clever in their own ways. Crows use tools, octopuses escape complicated containers, and chimpanzees can learn to use sticks to reach food. Their intelligence may look different from ours, but it shows that solving problems is useful across many branches of life.

*adaptation keeps life going*

Every species has traits that help it fit into its environment. Camels store energy for desert journeys, polar bears have thick fur, and frogs can use camouflage to disappear into their surroundings. Nature has produced countless solutions to the same basic challenge: how to live well in a changing world.

The more we learn about animals, the less separate we seem from them. Their lives may look wildly different from ours, but beneath the feathers, fur, scales, and shells are many familiar themes—care, curiosity, cooperation, and the simple urge to keep going.

Proposal: Inclusive Living Lab

Project Overview

The Inclusive Living Lab will develop and evaluate affordable, accessible technologies and community programs that improve autonomy, health, mobility, employment, and social participation for people with disabilities.

Research Goals

  • Identify everyday barriers across housing, transportation, healthcare, education, and employment.
  • Co-design practical solutions with people with diverse disabilities.
  • Measure improvements in independence, wellbeing, safety, and community participation.
  • Create guidelines that public agencies, employers, and service providers can adopt.

Methods

The project will use participatory research, interviews, accessibility audits, surveys, and six-month pilot studies. Participants will receive compensation and accessible research materials. Advisory groups led by disabled people will guide recruitment, design, data interpretation, and dissemination.

Potential Interventions

  • Low-cost home modifications and adaptive devices.
  • Accessible digital tools for scheduling, communication, and navigation.
  • Peer-support and independent-living programs.
  • Training for clinicians, employers, transport staff, and caregivers.

Evaluation

Outcomes will include self-reported quality of life, reduced isolation, increased access to essential services, time saved on daily tasks, employment or education participation, and participant-defined measures of success. Results will be disaggregated by disability type, age, gender, income, and location.

Ethics and Accessibility

The study will follow informed-consent, privacy, safeguarding, and data-minimization principles. All materials and sessions will be available in accessible formats, including captioning, screen-reader-compatible documents, plain-language summaries, interpretation, and remote participation.

Expected Impact

The project will produce tested interventions, an open-access implementation toolkit, policy recommendations, and a scalable model for disability-inclusive innovation. Creative pilot sites, including those informally labeled atlantis and constable, can demonstrate how solutions adapt to different communities.

# project proposal: ai for better education

## project summary

This project will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve teaching and learning in developing countries. The program will provide affordable digital learning tools for students and teachers. It will focus on local needs such as limited teacher availability and large class sizes.

## goals

- improve student learning outcomes
- support teachers with useful classroom tools
- expand access to high quality learning materials
- identify students who need additional support
- provide education in local languages
- reduce inequality between urban and rural schools

## key activities

### 1. adaptive learning systems

An AI learning platform will assess each student’s knowledge and progress. It will then recommend lessons and practice activities suited to the student’s needs. The platform will work on low cost devices and will support offline use.

### 2. teacher support tools

Teachers will receive AI tools that help create lesson plans and quizzes. The system will suggest activities based on the curriculum and student performance. Teachers will remain responsible for all final decisions.

### 3. local language resources

Machine learning will help translate and adapt educational materials into local languages. Local educators will review all content to ensure that it is accurate and culturally appropriate.

### 4. early support for struggling students

The system will analyze learning progress to identify students who may need extra help. Schools will use these signals to provide tutoring and personal support. The system will not make decisions about student promotion or exclusion.

### 5. professional development

Teachers will receive training in digital learning and responsible AI use. They will learn how to interpret system recommendations and protect student privacy.

## implementation plan

### phase one: research and design

The project team will work with ministries of education and local schools to identify priorities. The team will study available technology and create a pilot program with local partners.

### phase two: pilot program

The pilot will take place in selected urban and rural schools. It will include teacher training and community consultation. Researchers will measure student progress and gather feedback from teachers and families.

### phase three: evaluation and improvement

Independent researchers will evaluate learning outcomes and system performance. The team will improve the platform based on evidence and user feedback.

### phase four: expansion

Successful tools will be introduced to more schools. Governments and local organizations will receive support to manage training and long term operation.

## technology approach

The platform will use machine learning for learning recommendations and progress analysis. AI tools will assist with content creation and translation. The system will support offline access through local servers and mobile devices. Open standards will help schools avoid dependence on a single provider.

## equity and safety

Student data will be collected only when necessary. Schools will use strong security and clear consent procedures. Algorithms will be tested for bias across gender language region and disability. Families and teachers will be informed about how the system works. Human educators will oversee all important decisions.

## evaluation measures

The project will measure:

- reading and mathematics achievement
- student attendance and engagement
- teacher workload and satisfaction
- use of learning materials
- access for rural students
- participation across gender groups
- cost per student
- long term system sustainability

## expected results

The project is expected to improve basic learning skills and increase student engagement. Teachers will gain practical support and better information about student needs. Schools will gain access to more relevant learning materials. Governments will receive evidence that can guide future education policy.

## budget priorities

Funding will support platform development and device access. It will also cover teacher training and local content production. Other priorities will include data protection independent evaluation and technical support.

## conclusion

Responsible use of machine learning and AI can help developing countries improve education at scale. The project will combine technology with teacher leadership local knowledge and community participation. Its success will depend on equity privacy accountability and long term public investment.

**Reductions**

You might begin with the river—  
the Paraná, brown and broad,  
where Jesuits taught Guaraní children  
to read, sing, and carve saints from wood.

“Reductions,” they called the settlements,  
from *reducir*: to gather people in.  
Not a small word, really,  
when soldiers, slave hunters, and governors  
were always trying to scatter them.

In the plaza, bells marked the morning.  
There were fields of maize and yerba mate,  
workshops, orchards, a choir  
whose music traveled farther than maps.  
On feast days, the whole town turned out—  
drums, bright cloth, candles, a fiesta  
with children darting between the elders.

But history keeps its other hand visible.  
The priests still carried Rome in their pockets;  
the village still answered to rules  
written by men from somewhere else.  
Protection could feel like shelter  
and also like a locked gate.

Then came the treaties.  
Spain and Portugal drew a line  
through forests, fields, and graves.  
The Guaraní were told to move—  
as if a home were furniture,  
as if a church could simply be packed.

They resisted at Mbororé,  
and later in the Guaraní War,  
when bullets met bows beneath the trees.  
The reductions fell, not all at once,  
but like a song losing its singers.

Still, listen: a violin survives,  
a carved angel keeps one chipped wing,  
and somewhere a grandmother says  
her people were not merely “reduced.”  
They built, argued, prayed, planted,  
and danced—yes, danced—  
until the plaza filled again with fiesta,  
and the old bells found a human answer.

Hear now the word of our sovereign King, whose crown doth shine with heaven’s own light. By royal seal and solemn command, these mandates are proclaimed, that peace may flourish and disorder be cast into the shadows.

"Let \(x\) be the number of members with 3 pets.

- Those \(x\) members have \(3x\) pets.
- The other \(20-x\) members have at least 1 pet each.
- Total pets: \(3x+(20-x)=20+2x\).

Since there are 32 pets:

\[
20+2x\le 32
\]

\[
2x\le 12
\]

\[
x\le 6
\]

This is possible: 6 members have 3 pets each, and the remaining 14 members have 1 pet each, totaling \(18+14=32\) pets.

\[
\boxed{6}
\]"

# Project Proposal: AI for Better Education

## Project Summary

This project will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve education in developing countries. It will support teachers and students through affordable digital tools that work with limited internet access. The project will focus on personalized learning teacher support and better use of education data.

## Goals

- Improve student learning outcomes
- Expand access to quality learning materials
- Support teachers with practical classroom tools
- Identify students who need additional help
- Reduce education gaps between rural and urban communities

## Key Activities

### 1. Personalized Learning

An AI learning platform will assess each student’s knowledge and learning pace. It will recommend suitable lessons exercises and explanations. Content will be available in local languages where possible.

The platform will function offline through mobile phones tablets and local school servers. It will synchronize data whenever an internet connection becomes available.

### 2. Teacher Support

Teachers will receive AI assisted lesson planning tools. These tools will help create activities quizzes and reading materials that match national curriculum standards.

The system will also provide suggestions for explaining difficult topics. Teachers will remain responsible for all final decisions.

### 3. Early Identification of Learning Needs

Machine learning models will analyze student performance and attendance patterns. The system will identify students who may be falling behind.

Teachers and school leaders will receive clear alerts and recommended support actions. The project will protect student privacy and avoid using AI to make high stakes decisions without human review.

### 4. Local Learning Content

The project will work with local teachers universities and education ministries to create culturally relevant content. AI tools will assist with translation adaptation and content creation.

All materials will be reviewed by qualified educators before they are shared with students.

### 5. School Data Systems

Simple data systems will help schools track attendance progress and resource needs. Education officials will use aggregated information to plan teacher training and distribute resources more effectively.

## Implementation Plan

### Phase One: Research and Design

The project team will study local education needs infrastructure language requirements and existing policies. Teachers students and community leaders will participate in the design process.

### Phase Two: Pilot Program

The project will launch in a small number of schools across urban rural and remote communities. The pilot will test usability learning impact cost and technical reliability.

### Phase Three: Evaluation

Student outcomes will be compared with results from similar schools that do not use the new tools. Feedback will be collected from teachers students families and administrators.

### Phase Four: Expansion

Successful tools will be improved and introduced to additional schools. Local institutions will receive training so they can manage the systems and adapt the content.

## Equity and Ethics

The project will prioritize equal access. Devices and offline options will support students who lack reliable internet access.

Data will be collected only when necessary. It will be stored securely and governed by clear privacy rules. Families will receive information about how data is used.

AI systems will be tested for bias across gender language disability income level and location. Human educators will oversee recommendations and correct harmful or inaccurate results.

## Expected Results

- Higher student engagement
- Improved reading and mathematics skills
- Faster support for students who are struggling
- More effective lesson preparation
- Better access to quality education in remote areas
- Stronger education planning through reliable data

## Budget Priorities

Funding will support software development teacher training local content creation devices offline infrastructure evaluation and long term technical support.

The project will use open standards and affordable technology to reduce dependence on expensive vendors.

## Sustainability

Local teachers and education institutions will be trained to manage and improve the tools. Partnerships with governments universities nonprofit organizations and telecommunications providers will support long term growth.

The project will measure cost per student and learning gains to ensure that future expansion remains practical.

## Conclusion

Machine learning and AI can strengthen education when they are designed around local needs and guided by teachers. This project will combine technology human expertise and community participation to deliver more personalized and equitable learning opportunities in developing countries.

World War II or the Second World War, often abbreviated as WWII or WW2, was a global conflict that lasted from 1939 to 1945. The vast majority of the world's countries, including all of the great powers, fought as part of two opposing military alliances: the Allies and the Axis. Many participants threw their economic, industrial, and scientific capabilities behind this total war, blurring the distinction between civilian and military resources. Aircraft played a major role, enabling the strategic bombing of population centres and the delivery of the only two nuclear weapons ever used in war. World War II was by far the deadliest conflict in history, resulting in an estimated 70 to 85 million fatalities, mostly among civilians. Tens of millions died due to genocides (including the Holocaust), starvation, massacres, and disease. In the wake of Axis defeat, Germany, Austria and Japan were occupied, and war crimes tribunals were conducted against German and Japanese leaders.

*Why Animals Have More in Common Than We Think*

When you look at a dog, a dolphin, and a dragonfly, they seem like they belong to completely different worlds. But underneath the fur, fins, and wings, animals share surprising similarities.

*1. Everyone Needs a Good Meal*

All animals need energy to survive. Whether it’s grass for a cow, fish for a seal, or nectar for a butterfly, eating keeps bodies moving and growing. Even animals with very different diets follow the same basic rule: find food, digest it, and turn it into energy.

*2. Communication Is Everywhere*

Animals are constantly sending messages. Birds sing, wolves howl, ants leave scent trails, and bees dance to show where food is. Humans use words and gestures, but the goal is often the same: warn others, attract a mate, defend territory, or stay connected.

*3. Family Matters*

Many animals care for their young. Elephants protect calves, penguins take turns keeping eggs warm, and birds bring food back to their nests. Even animals that live alone may spend a lot of time protecting or teaching their babies.

*4. Animals Learn and Adapt*

Animals aren’t simply running on instinct. Crows can solve puzzles, octopuses open containers, and young monkeys learn by watching adults. Across species, experience helps animals figure out what works—and what to avoid next time.

*5. Everyone Needs Rest*

Sleep and rest are common across the animal kingdom. Cats may nap for most of the day, while dolphins rest one half of their brains at a time. The details differ, but animals need downtime to recover, process information, and stay healthy.

*6. Social Lives Can Be Complicated*

Animals form friendships, rivalries, teams, and groups. Chimpanzees cooperate, horses develop preferences for certain companions, and whales travel in close family pods. Their social worlds may not look exactly like ours, but they can be just as rich.

*The Big Connection*

The animal kingdom is full of variety, but the same basic needs keep appearing: food, safety, communication, family, learning, and rest. Looking for these similarities makes animals feel less like strangers—and reminds us that life has more shared patterns than we often realize.

# Project Proposal: AI for Inclusive Education

## Project Overview

This project will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve the quality of education in developing countries. The program will support teachers and students with affordable digital tools that work in local languages and function in areas with limited internet access.

## Goals

- Improve student learning outcomes
- Provide personalized learning support
- Strengthen teacher training
- Expand access to high quality educational materials
- Reduce barriers caused by poverty distance disability and language

## Key Activities

### 1. Personalized Learning

An AI learning platform will assess each student’s skills and provide lessons suited to their level. The system will identify learning gaps and recommend practice activities. Students will receive immediate feedback through phones tablets or community learning centers.

### 2. Teacher Support

Teachers will receive AI assisted lesson plans assessment tools and classroom guidance. The system will help educators identify students who need additional support. Training modules will help teachers use digital tools effectively while preserving the importance of human judgment.

### 3. Local Language Content

Machine learning tools will help translate and adapt educational resources into local languages. Content will reflect local history culture and community needs. Educators will review all generated materials before they are used in classrooms.

### 4. Offline Access

The platform will be designed for low bandwidth environments. Educational content will be available through offline servers memory cards basic mobile phones and local networks. Data will synchronize whenever an internet connection becomes available.

### 5. Early Warning Systems

AI models will identify students at risk of falling behind or leaving school. Signals may include attendance patterns assessment results and learning activity. Schools will use these insights to provide timely counseling tutoring or family support.

## Implementation Plan

The project will begin with pilot programs in selected rural and urban communities. Local schools ministries universities and nonprofit organizations will help design and test the system. The first phase will focus on mathematics literacy and teacher development.

After the pilot phase the program will be improved using evidence from students teachers and families. Successful tools will then expand to additional regions. Local staff will receive technical training so that communities can manage the system over time.

## Equity and Safety

The project will protect student privacy through secure data storage limited data collection and clear consent procedures. AI will support educators rather than replace them. Regular audits will check for bias related to gender language disability income or geography.

Devices and services will be offered through schools and community centers so that students without personal technology can participate. Special attention will be given to girls students with disabilities and displaced learners.

## Evaluation

Success will be measured through:

- Reading and mathematics achievement
- Student attendance and retention
- Teacher confidence and effectiveness
- Use of learning materials
- Access among underserved groups
- Cost per student
- Family and community satisfaction

Independent researchers will compare participating schools with similar schools that do not yet use the program.

## Expected Impact

The project will help students learn at their own pace and give teachers practical support. It will expand access to quality resources and allow education systems to respond more quickly to local needs. By combining responsible AI with strong community leadership the program can improve learning while building sustainable digital capacity.

## Budget Priorities

Funding will support platform development teacher training local content creation devices connectivity research privacy protection and long term technical support. Partnerships with governments universities technology organizations and philanthropic groups will reduce costs and improve sustainability.

# Project Proposal: AI for Better Education

## Project Summary

This project will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve education in developing countries. The program will support teachers and learners through affordable digital tools that work with limited internet access. It will focus on personalized learning teacher support language access and better education planning.

## Goals

1. Improve student learning outcomes.
2. Provide learning support for students who lack qualified teachers.
3. Help teachers plan lessons and identify learning gaps.
4. Expand access to quality education in rural and underserved communities.
5. Reduce inequality linked to poverty language disability and gender.

## Main Activities

### 1. Personalized Learning

An AI learning platform will assess each student’s current skills. It will recommend lessons exercises and explanations that match the student’s needs. The system will adjust difficulty as the student improves.

The platform will support local languages and low cost mobile devices. It will also provide offline content that can be updated when a device connects to the internet.

### 2. Teacher Support

Teachers will receive tools that help them create lesson plans quizzes and learning materials. AI will summarize student performance and highlight areas that need attention.

The system will not replace teachers. It will reduce administrative work and give teachers more time to support students directly.

### 3. Early Warning Systems

Machine learning models will identify students who may be at risk of falling behind or leaving school. Signals may include attendance changes assignment results and declining participation.

Schools can then provide tutoring counseling transportation support or other assistance.

### 4. Local Learning Content

The project will work with local educators to create culturally relevant content. AI can help translate materials into local languages and adapt examples to local communities.

All content will be reviewed by qualified educators before use.

### 5. Education Planning

Governments and education partners will receive dashboards that show trends in enrollment attendance learning outcomes and teacher needs. These insights can support better decisions about funding staffing and school resources.

## Implementation Plan

### Phase One: Research and Design

The project team will consult students teachers families and education officials. It will identify local needs device access language requirements and privacy risks.

### Phase Two: Pilot Program

The tools will be tested in a small group of urban rural and remote schools. Teachers will receive training and regular technical support.

### Phase Three: Evaluation

Researchers will compare student outcomes with results from similar schools that do not use the tools. The evaluation will measure learning progress attendance teacher workload equity and user satisfaction.

### Phase Four: Expansion

Successful tools will be improved and expanded through partnerships with ministries of education schools universities nonprofit groups and telecommunications providers.

## Equity and Safety

The project will protect student privacy through data minimization secure storage and clear consent procedures. Student data will not be sold or used for unrelated purposes.

AI recommendations will be reviewed for bias. Students will always have access to human teachers and support staff. The program will include accessibility features for learners with disabilities.

## Expected Results

Within three years the project aims to:

- Improve reading and mathematics performance.
- Increase student attendance and engagement.
- Reduce teacher administrative workload.
- Expand access to high quality learning materials.
- Improve early support for students at risk.
- Strengthen evidence based education planning.

## Budget Priorities

Funding will support software development teacher training local content creation device access internet solutions evaluation cybersecurity and long term maintenance.

## Conclusion

AI can help improve education when it is designed around local needs and guided by teachers. This project will combine machine learning with human expertise to deliver affordable inclusive and effective learning support. Its success will depend on strong community participation responsible data practices and sustained public investment.

# Project Proposal: AI for Better Education

## Project Overview

This project will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve education in developing countries. The program will support teachers and students through affordable digital tools that work in local languages and in areas with limited internet access.

## Main Goals

- Improve student learning outcomes
- Support teachers with useful classroom resources
- Expand access to high quality education
- Identify learning gaps at an early stage
- Reduce inequality between urban and rural schools

## Key Activities

### 1. Adaptive Learning Platforms

We will develop mobile and web based learning platforms that adjust lessons to each student’s needs. The system will assess progress and provide practice at an appropriate level.

### 2. Teacher Support Tools

AI tools will help teachers create lesson plans quizzes and learning activities. Teachers will remain responsible for final decisions while the system reduces routine preparation work.

### 3. Local Language Resources

Machine learning models will help translate and produce educational content in local languages. Community educators will review all materials to ensure cultural accuracy and clarity.

### 4. Early Warning Systems

The project will analyze attendance results and participation patterns to identify students who may need extra support. Schools can then provide tutoring mentoring or other targeted assistance.

### 5. Offline Access

The platform will store lessons on low cost devices and local school servers. Students and teachers will be able to use core features without continuous internet access.

## Implementation Plan

The project will begin with a pilot in selected schools. We will consult teachers families education officials and local organizations before development begins. After testing we will improve the tools and expand them to additional regions.

Training will be provided for teachers school leaders and technical staff. Local partners will help manage content privacy and long term maintenance.

## Expected Results

- Higher reading and mathematics achievement
- More effective teacher preparation
- Greater student engagement
- Faster support for struggling learners
- Increased access to relevant learning materials
- Stronger education systems in underserved communities

## Ethics and Safety

Student data will be protected through strict privacy rules. The system will collect only necessary information and will use secure storage. Human educators will supervise important decisions. Regular audits will check for bias errors and unequal treatment.

## Evaluation

Success will be measured through student assessments attendance teacher feedback and school participation. Results from pilot schools will be compared with results from similar schools that do not yet use the program. Findings will guide future improvements and funding decisions.

## Budget Priorities

Funding will support software development device access teacher training local content creation data protection evaluation and technical support. The project will favor open standards and affordable technology so that schools can continue using the system after initial funding ends.

## Conclusion

AI can strengthen education when it is designed around local needs and guided by teachers. This project will combine machine learning with human expertise to give more students access to effective personalized and inclusive learning.

To write a good Chinese poem:

1. **Begin with a precise image**  
   Show a moonlit window, falling leaves, or an empty road instead of simply saying “I feel sad.”

2. **Use concise language**  
   Chinese poetry gains strength from brevity. Remove words that do not add sound, meaning, or emotion.

3. **Create emotional movement**  
   Let the poem shift—from observation to memory, calm to longing, or darkness to hope.

4. **Pay attention to sound and rhythm**  
   Read the poem aloud. Balance short and long phrases, and use rhyme or repeated sounds naturally.

5. **Use imagery and contrast**  
   Pair opposites such as light and shadow, near and far, silence and sound.

6. **Leave space for interpretation**  
   Avoid explaining every feeling. A strong ending often suggests more than it states.

7. **Revise carefully**  
   Replace vague adjectives with concrete nouns and verbs. Read it aloud several times and cut anything unnecessary.

A simple structure is:

> **Image → association → emotional turn → memorable ending**

For example:

> 秋灯照旧砚，  
> 雨过小窗寒。  
> 欲写归乡字，  
> 风先到故山。

P.S. Read excellent classical and modern Chinese poems widely, then imitate their techniques before developing your own voice.

Inclusive LifeLab: Designing Better Everyday Lives for People with Disabilities

Executive Summary

This project will investigate how accessible technology, inclusive public services, and community-led design can improve quality of life for people with disabilities. The study will combine lived-experience research with measurable outcomes in health, independence, social participation, employment, and personal wellbeing.

Research Question

Which combinations of environmental changes, assistive technologies, and social supports produce the greatest improvements in daily autonomy and wellbeing for people with diverse disabilities?

Objectives

  • Identify barriers affecting mobility, communication, employment, education, and social connection.
  • Co-design practical interventions with disabled participants, caregivers, service providers, and policymakers.
  • Evaluate whether interventions improve independence, satisfaction, participation, and mental health.
  • Develop an implementation toolkit that communities can adapt and scale.

Methodology

  1. Needs assessment: Conduct accessible surveys, interviews, focus groups, and diary studies with participants across age groups, disability types, income levels, and geographic settings.
  2. Co-design: Establish paid advisory panels led by people with disabilities. Participants will help prioritize problems and design potential solutions.
  3. Pilot interventions: Test selected solutions, such as accessible transit information, adaptive workplace tools, peer-support networks, and simplified service navigation.
  4. Evaluation: Use a mixed-methods design, comparing baseline and post-intervention measures over 12 months alongside qualitative accounts of participants’ experiences.

Measures of Success

  • Improved self-reported quality of life and autonomy.
  • Greater participation in work, education, recreation, and civic life.
  • Reduced time and cost required to access essential services.
  • Higher satisfaction with accessibility and support systems.
  • Evidence that benefits are equitable across disability, gender, age, and socioeconomic groups.

Ethics and Accessibility

The project will use informed consent in accessible formats, fair participant compensation, privacy-protective data practices, and ongoing review by a disability-led ethics advisory group. All research materials, meetings, and digital tools will be designed for accessibility from the outset.

Expected Outcomes

The project will produce evidence-based recommendations, an open implementation toolkit, policy briefs, and prototype solutions that communities can adopt. It will also establish a reusable research framework for inclusive innovation. Creative naming and visual materials may draw on themes such as atlantis and constable, while keeping the project’s practical focus on dignity, access, and self-determination.

Proposed Timeline

  • Months 1–3: Partnership building, ethics approval, and accessible needs assessment.
  • Months 4–8: Data collection and co-design workshops.
  • Months 9–18: Pilot implementation and outcome evaluation.
  • Months 19–21: Analysis and community validation.
  • Months 22–24: Dissemination, toolkit publication, and policy engagement.

Conclusion

Inclusive LifeLab will shift disability research from studying people as problems to partnering with people as experts. By combining rigorous evaluation with community leadership, the project aims to generate practical changes that make everyday life more accessible, autonomous, and fulfilling.

The remaining \(20-x\) members have at least 1 pet each. Thus, the total number of pets is at least

\[
3x + (20-x) = 20+2x.
\]

Since there are 32 pets,

\[
20+2x \le 32
\]

\[
2x \le 12
\]

\[
x \le 6.
\]

Therefore, the maximum number of members who can have 3 pets is \(\boxed{6}\)."

# Why the Canucks Need to Be More Mindful of Their Environment

By Naomi

For the Vancouver Canucks, success is shaped by more than skill, strategy, and determination. The environments surrounding the team also play an important role. From the locker room and training facilities to the arena, travel routines, and the wider Vancouver community, every setting can influence focus, confidence, health, and performance.

A mindful environment begins with awareness. Players and staff need spaces that support recovery, communication, and preparation. A calm locker room can help athletes reset after a difficult game. A well-designed training space can encourage concentration and reduce unnecessary stress. Even small details—lighting, noise, cleanliness, temperature, and access to healthy food—can affect how people feel and perform.

The team’s environment also includes its relationships. Respectful communication between players, coaches, medical staff, and management creates trust. When people feel heard and valued, they are more likely to speak openly about fatigue, injuries, pressure, or concerns. That openness can help prevent problems before they grow and can strengthen the team’s unity.

Mindfulness should extend beyond the rink. The Canucks are deeply connected to Vancouver and its diverse communities. Being attentive to local needs, environmental sustainability, and the experiences of fans can help the organization act as a responsible member of the city. Reducing waste, using resources thoughtfully, and supporting community initiatives are practical ways to make a positive difference.

Players also benefit from becoming more aware of their personal environments. Paying attention to sleep, travel conditions, digital distractions, nutrition, and emotional wellbeing can improve preparation. Hockey is demanding, and small habits can have a meaningful effect over a long season.

Being mindful does not mean seeking perfection. It means noticing what is happening, understanding how surroundings affect people, and making thoughtful improvements. For the Canucks, this approach could support stronger performance, healthier relationships, and a deeper connection with their fans and community.

A team that pays attention to its environment is better prepared to adapt, grow, and succeed—both on the ice and beyond it.
