# Project Proposal: AI for Better Education

## Project Title

**Learning Forward**

## Overview

Learning Forward will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve education in developing countries. The project will support teachers and students through affordable digital tools. It will focus on local needs and work within limits such as weak internet access and limited school funding.

## Goals

- Improve student learning outcomes
- Support teachers with useful classroom tools
- Expand access to high quality learning materials
- Identify students who need extra support
- Reduce educational inequality
- Strengthen local education systems

## Main Activities

### 1. Adaptive Learning

An AI learning platform will adjust lessons based on each student’s progress. Students will receive practice tasks at an appropriate level. The system will provide explanations and feedback in local languages when possible.

### 2. Teacher Support

Teachers will receive an AI assistant that can help create lesson plans. It can suggest activities and generate quizzes. It can also explain difficult topics and recommend support for students who are falling behind.

Teachers will remain responsible for all final decisions. The AI will support professional judgment rather than replace it.

### 3. Early Support for Students

Machine learning models will review learning data to identify students who may need additional help. Schools can then provide tutoring or other support before learning gaps become severe.

The system will use only necessary data. Student information will be protected through strong security and clear privacy rules.

### 4. Offline Access

The project will create tools that work on low cost phones and basic computers. Learning materials will be available offline through local servers or memory cards. Devices can update their content whenever an internet connection becomes available.

### 5. Local Content Creation

Local teachers and education experts will help develop lessons. AI tools can assist with translation and adaptation. Every lesson will be reviewed by qualified people to ensure accuracy and cultural relevance.

## Implementation Plan

### Phase One: Research

The project team will study local education challenges. This will include school visits and discussions with teachers and families. The team will identify priority subjects and languages.

### Phase Two: Pilot Program

The project will launch in a small group of schools. Teachers will receive training. Students will use the learning platform during selected lessons. Researchers will measure learning progress and collect feedback.

### Phase Three: Improvement

The team will improve the tools based on evidence from the pilot. Problems related to language access usability and fairness will be addressed.

### Phase Four: Expansion

The project will expand to more schools through partnerships with governments universities nonprofits and community groups.

## Training and Support

Teachers will receive practical training in digital skills and AI literacy. School leaders will learn how to use learning data responsibly. Local technical staff will receive training so schools can maintain the system without depending entirely on outside experts.

## Ethics and Safety

The project will follow strict principles.

- Protect student privacy
- Seek informed permission from families
- Avoid unfair treatment by automated systems
- Explain how AI recommendations are made
- Provide human review for important decisions
- Test systems for bias
- Keep educational content accurate
- Ensure access for students with disabilities

AI will never determine a student’s future alone. Teachers and families will remain involved in important choices.

## Evaluation

Success will be measured through:

- Reading and mathematics improvement
- Student attendance
- Student engagement
- Teacher workload
- Teacher confidence
- Access to learning materials
- Use across different languages and communities
- Progress among disadvantaged students

Independent evaluators will compare participating schools with similar schools that do not use the program.

## Expected Results

The project is expected to improve basic skills and increase student engagement. Teachers will gain more time for personal guidance. Schools will receive better information about student needs. Governments will gain evidence that can guide future education policy.

## Budget Priorities

Funding will support:

- Device access
- Offline technology
- Teacher training
- Local content development
- System maintenance
- Privacy and security
- Independent evaluation
- Community engagement

## Conclusion

Learning Forward will combine human expertise with responsible AI. Its purpose is not to replace teachers. Its purpose is to help teachers reach more students with better support. By using affordable technology and local leadership the project can improve education quality and create stronger opportunities for children in developing countries.

Project Proposal: Inclusive Living Lab

\\n\\n

Overview

\\n

\\n The Inclusive Living Lab will investigate practical, scalable ways to improve quality of life for people with disabilities by combining accessible technology, community-based services, and participatory research. People with disabilities will guide the project\\u2019s priorities, design, testing, and evaluation.\\n

\\n\\n

Research Question

\\n

\\n Which combinations of assistive technologies, environmental adaptations, and social supports produce the greatest improvements in independence, wellbeing, participation, and access to education and employment?\\n

\\n\\n

Objectives

\\n
    \\n
  • Identify everyday barriers affecting mobility, communication, healthcare, housing, and social participation.
    • \\n
  • Co-design affordable interventions with disabled participants, caregivers, and service providers.
    • \\n
  • Evaluate outcomes over 12 months using both quantitative and lived-experience measures.
    • \\n
  • Develop evidence-based recommendations for policymakers, employers, schools, and technology developers.
    • \\n
\\n\\n

Methods

\\n
    \\n
  1. Discovery: Conduct interviews, accessibility audits, surveys, and community workshops across diverse disability groups.
    2. \\n
  2. Co-design: Create prototypes such as adaptive home controls, accessible transit tools, communication supports, and personalized service-navigation platforms.
    3. \\n
  3. Pilot testing: Test selected interventions with 150 participants in urban, suburban, and rural communities.
    4. \\n
  4. Evaluation: Measure independence, mental wellbeing, social connection, time use, cost, accessibility, and participant satisfaction.
    5. \\n
  5. Implementation: Publish open standards, practical toolkits, and policy guidance for replication.
    6. \\n
\\n\\n

Ethics and Inclusion

\\n

\\n The project will use accessible consent materials, fair compensation, privacy-preserving data practices, and an advisory board led primarily by people with disabilities. Participation will be voluntary, and research outputs will be available in accessible formats, including plain language, captions, transcripts, screen-reader-compatible documents, and sign-language interpretation where needed.\\n

\\n\\n

Expected Impact

\\n

\\n The project aims to produce measurable improvements in independence and wellbeing while reducing avoidable costs and exclusion. It will also create a reusable framework for evaluating accessibility interventions across different communities and disability experiences.\\n

\\n\\n

Timeline and Deliverables

\\n
    \\n
  • Months 1\\u20133: Community consultation and baseline assessment.
    • \\n
  • Months 4\\u20138: Co-design and prototype development.
    • \\n
  • Months 9\\u201320: Pilot implementation and evaluation.
    • \\n
  • Months 21\\u201324: Analysis, dissemination, and policy recommendations.
    • \\n
\\n\\n

写好一首中文诗，可以从以下几方面入手：

1. **先确定核心情感**  
   先想清楚要写什么：思乡、离别、爱情、孤独、喜悦，或对自然的感受。情感越具体，诗越动人。

2. **用具体意象表达**  
   少直接说“我很悲伤”，多写“空阶一夜雨”“灯影照无眠”。月、雁、江、秋风等传统意象可以使用，但最好赋予它们个人 अनुभव。

3. **锤炼语言**  
   中文诗讲究简洁、含蓄和节奏。删去无关的字，选择准确有力的动词。例如“风吹树叶”可改为“风翻碎叶”。

4. **重视节奏与声音**  
   朗读诗句，注意停顿、平仄、押韵和音节长度。古体诗、近体诗需要遵守相应格律；现代诗则更注重自然的呼吸和内在节奏。

5. **营造画面与转折**  
   让诗中有可见、可听、可感的场景，并在结尾形成新的理解或余韵。好的结尾不一定解释，而是留下回声。

6. **避免空泛和堆砌**  
   华丽词藻不等于诗意。每个意象都应服务于情感，避免为了“像诗”而生硬押韵。

7. **反复修改**  
   写完后大声朗读，删掉最普通的一句，替换最模糊的词，并检查每一行是否不可替代。

可以尝试这个简单结构：

> 一个具体场景  
> 一个触发情感的细节  
> 一个意象的变化  
> 一个含蓄而有余味的结尾

**P.S.** 好诗不在于词藻多么华丽，而在于用最准确的语言，让读者看见你独特的感受。

Proposal: Inclusive Futures

Project Overview

Inclusive Futures is a participatory research project designed to identify, test, and scale practical solutions that improve quality of life for people with disabilities. The project will focus on autonomy, health, social connection, employment, mobility, and access to public services.

Research Questions

  • Which environmental, technological, and social barriers most affect daily wellbeing?
  • Which interventions produce measurable improvements in independence and life satisfaction?
  • How can communities design services with disabled people rather than for them?
  • How do needs differ across disability types, ages, income levels, and cultural contexts?

Methodology

  1. Community partnership: Establish an advisory board led primarily by people with lived experience of disability.
  2. Needs assessment: Conduct accessible surveys, interviews, focus groups, mobility diaries, and service-journey mapping.
  3. Co-design: Develop solutions such as accessible transit tools, flexible employment supports, peer-navigation services, and adaptive home technologies.
  4. Pilot testing: Run 12-month pilots in urban, suburban, and rural communities.
  5. Evaluation: Measure changes in wellbeing, independence, participation, service access, cost, and user satisfaction.

Innovative Component

The project will create an open, privacy-protective platform called Atlantis that lets participants report barriers, track outcomes, and share recommendations with researchers, service providers, and policymakers. A practical implementation framework, named Constable, will help organizations assess accessibility, accountability, and long-term sustainability.

Ethics and Accessibility

  • Obtain informed consent in multiple accessible formats.
  • Compensate participants fairly for their time and expertise.
  • Protect personal data and allow participants to withdraw at any time.
  • Provide sign-language interpretation, captioning, screen-reader-compatible materials, transportation support, and flexible participation options.

Expected Outcomes

The project will produce evidence-based recommendations, tested community interventions, an accessibility measurement toolkit, and policy guidance. Success will be defined by meaningful improvements in participants’ autonomy, wellbeing, social inclusion, and ability to access education, work, healthcare, transportation, and civic life.

Timeline and Budget Categories

The proposed timeline is 30 months: six months for preparation, 12 months for research and co-design, 12 months for pilots, and six months for analysis and dissemination. Major budget categories include participant compensation, accessibility services, research staff, technology development, pilot delivery, evaluation, and knowledge sharing.

Impact

By placing disabled people at the center of decision-making, Inclusive Futures will move beyond identifying barriers and demonstrate which solutions work, for whom, and under what conditions. The findings will support more inclusive communities and guide funders, employers, healthcare providers, technology developers, and governments toward measurable improvements in quality of life.

# Project Proposal: AI for Better Education in Developing Countries

## Project Overview

This project will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve learning outcomes in underserved communities. The program will provide personalized learning tools for students and practical support for teachers. It will focus on low cost technology that can work with limited internet access.

## Goals

- Improve student reading and mathematics skills
- Provide personalized lessons based on each student’s needs
- Support teachers with planning and assessment tools
- Expand access to high quality learning materials
- Reduce education gaps between urban and rural communities

## Main Activities

### 1. Personalized Learning

An AI platform will assess each student’s knowledge and learning pace. It will then recommend suitable lessons exercises and explanations. The platform will adjust difficulty as the student improves.

### 2. Teacher Support

Teachers will receive tools that help create lesson plans quizzes and practice activities. AI will identify common student errors and suggest ways to address them. Teachers will remain responsible for final decisions.

### 3. Local Language Content

The project will develop learning materials in local languages. AI translation tools will help adapt content to regional needs. Local educators will review all materials for accuracy and cultural relevance.

### 4. Offline Access

The platform will support smartphones tablets and basic computers. Lessons will be stored locally so students can learn without continuous internet access. Data will synchronize when a connection becomes available.

### 5. Early Warning System

Machine learning will identify students who may be at risk of falling behind or leaving school. Schools can then provide tutoring mentoring or family support.

## Implementation Plan

The project will begin with a pilot in selected schools. These schools will represent different regions and levels of connectivity. Baseline data will be collected before launch.

During the pilot teachers will receive training and ongoing support. Student progress will be measured through regular assessments. Feedback from students teachers families and education officials will guide improvements.

After the pilot the strongest tools will be expanded to more schools. Partnerships with governments universities nonprofit groups and technology providers will support long term growth.

## Equity and Safety

The project will protect student privacy through secure data systems and strict access controls. It will avoid using sensitive data unless necessary. AI recommendations will be reviewed by educators.

The program will monitor for bias related to language gender disability income and location. Schools will receive non digital alternatives for students who lack devices or reliable electricity.

## Expected Results

- Higher reading and mathematics performance
- Better teacher preparation
- Faster identification of learning difficulties
- Greater access to quality educational content
- Improved participation among rural students
- Stronger education planning through reliable data

## Evaluation

Success will be measured through student assessments teacher surveys attendance records and school completion data. Results will be compared with similar schools that do not yet use the system.

The project will also measure access reliability cost student engagement and fairness across different groups.

## Budget Priorities

Funding will support software development teacher training local content creation devices connectivity technical support research and independent evaluation. The project will prioritize open standards and affordable tools to reduce long term costs.

## Conclusion

AI can help developing countries provide more effective and inclusive education. The proposed project combines technology with teacher expertise local knowledge and strong safeguards. Its purpose is not to replace educators. Its purpose is to give every learner a better chance to succeed.

A professional sports team has a powerful platform, and its actions can influence the wider Vancouver community.

Most importantly, mindfulness helps the team stay present. By noticing what is happening around them, the Canucks can respond more effectively, protect their well-being, and build a stronger culture. Awareness of the environment is not a distraction from performance—it is part of performance.

The Canucks have the talent, commitment, and community support to make a difference. By becoming more mindful of their environments, they can create better conditions for success on the ice and set a positive example far beyond it.

# Interesting Facts About the Dutch Language

Dutch is spoken by more than 25 million people, primarily in the Netherlands and Belgium. It is also an official language in Suriname and several Caribbean islands, including Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten.

## A Language Between English and German

Dutch belongs to the West Germanic language family, alongside English and German. This relationship is easy to see in familiar words. For example, the Dutch word *water* resembles the English word “water,” while *boek* is similar to German *Buch* and English “book.”

Dutch often acts as a linguistic bridge between English and German. Its grammar and vocabulary share features with both languages, although Dutch has its own distinct pronunciation and spelling rules.

## Dutch Has Some Very Long Words

Dutch is famous for its ability to combine multiple words into one. A well-known example is *kindercarnavalsoptochtvoorbereidingswerkzaamhedenplan*, meaning “plan for the preparations for a children’s carnival procession.” While such words are uncommon in everyday conversation, they demonstrate how flexible Dutch word formation can be.

*Dutch speakers can create compound words whenever they need to describe a complex idea clearly and precisely.*

## The Famous “G” Sound

One of the most recognizable features of Dutch is its throaty “g” sound, especially in the northern Netherlands. This sound is produced toward the back of the throat and can be challenging for learners.

However, pronunciation varies by region. In much of Belgium and the southern Netherlands, the “g” is often softer and less guttural. This difference is sometimes used to distinguish northern Dutch from Belgian Dutch.

## Dutch and Afrikaans Are Closely Related

Afrikaans, spoken mainly in South Africa and Namibia, developed from Dutch brought to southern Africa by settlers in the seventeenth century. The two languages remain similar in vocabulary and sentence structure.

For instance, the Dutch phrase *Ik heb een boek* corresponds closely to the Afrikaans phrase *Ek het ’n boek*, both meaning “I have a book.” Although Dutch and Afrikaans are not mutually identical, speakers can often recognize many words and expressions in the other language.

## Words Dutch Gave to English

English contains many words borrowed from Dutch, especially through trade, exploration, and naval history. Examples include:

- *Yacht* from Dutch *jacht*
- *Cookie* from *koekje*
- *Landscape* from *landschap*
- *Freight* from *vracht*
- *Boss* from *baas*
- *Coleslaw* from *koolsla*

The influence was particularly strong during the seventeenth century, when Dutch merchants and sailors played a major role in global commerce.

## Dutch Has Two Words for “You”

Dutch uses *jij* or *je* for informal “you” and *u* for formal “you.” The choice depends on the relationship between speakers and the social situation.

Although modern Dutch has become more informal in many settings, *u* is still commonly used when speaking to strangers, older people, customers, or someone in a formal position.

## A Language with Regional Variety

Dutch spoken in the Netherlands and Dutch spoken in Belgium are both standard forms of the language, but they differ in accent, vocabulary, and sometimes pronunciation. Belgian Dutch is often called Flemish, although “Flemish” can also refer more broadly to the Dutch dialects of Flanders.

Despite these differences, speakers from the Netherlands and Belgium generally understand one another very well.

## A Rich Vocabulary for Everyday Life

Dutch has many expressive words that are difficult to translate with a single English equivalent. *Gezellig*, for example, describes a warm, comfortable, friendly atmosphere or experience. It might refer to a cozy café, a pleasant gathering with friends, or an inviting home.

Another interesting word is *uitwaaien*, which means going outside—often to the coast or countryside—to enjoy fresh air and clear one’s mind.

*These words show how languages reflect the experiences and values of the cultures that speak them.*

## Conclusion

Dutch is a fascinating language with deep historical roots, regional diversity, creative word formation, and connections to languages around the world. Whether you are interested in linguistics, travel, history, or literature, learning about Dutch offers an enjoyable glimpse into the culture of the Netherlands, Belgium, Suriname, and beyond.

“Come in from the forest; we’ll build a new day.”  
The Church called them *reductions*—not smaller souls,  
but towns where the scattered could gather as whole.

In Paraguay, beneath the red-earth sky,  
bells rang at dawn and the markets grew high.  
They learned Latin hymns, carved saints from wood,  
and planted their fields as a community should.

But don’t picture peace as a permanent fiesta—  
there were orders from kings, and a governor’s vista,  
soldiers who came saying, “These people are ours,”  
and families hiding through long, frightened hours.

Still, on feast days, the drums answered the choir;  
the plaza shone gold in the candlelight’s fire.  
One child asked, “Father, will this last?”  
He paused, then replied, “We’ll make it last.”

So history keeps both the wound and the song,  
the welcome, the power, the times things went wrong.  
A reduction, they called it—yet here, in the street,  
people made room for each other to meet.

And somewhere a grandmother, laughing, says, “Fiesta!”  
While bells tell the dusk that the day has been blessed.  
The word travels onward, through sorrow and grace:  
Fiesta, again—make the world a shared place.

*Same Needs, Different Bodies*

Animals may look wildly different, but many of them have surprisingly similar lives. Whether they have feathers, fur, scales, or shells, most animals are trying to do the same basic things: find food, stay safe, communicate, and raise their young.

*Everyone Needs a Home*

From birds building nests to rabbits digging burrows, animals create spaces where they can rest and protect themselves. Bees live in hives, wolves gather in dens, and even tiny insects make careful shelters. A home can be a tree hollow, a coral reef, or a patch of grass—it just needs to provide safety.

*Communication Is Everywhere*

Animals are constantly sending messages. Dogs bark, whales sing, ants leave scent trails, and bees dance to point out food. These signals may seem strange to us, but they help animals warn each other, attract mates, defend territory, and stay connected.

*Families Look Familiar*

Many species take care of their young in ways that feel familiar. Birds feed their chicks, elephants protect calves, and wolves teach pups how to survive. Some animals spend years raising their offspring, while others provide only brief care, but the goal is similar: give the next generation a better chance.

*Play Isn’t Just for Pets*

Play appears across the animal kingdom. Young otters tumble in the water, monkeys chase each other through trees, and fox kits wrestle in the grass. Play helps animals practice important skills, build relationships, and explore their surroundings.

*Teamwork Makes Life Easier*

Animals often cooperate to solve problems. Meerkats take turns watching for danger, dolphins work together to catch fish, and birds may flock to confuse predators. Even species that compete sometimes cooperate when working together improves everyone’s chances.

*Adaptation Connects Us All*

Every animal has traits that help it survive. A camel stores energy for dry environments, a polar bear has thick fur for the cold, and a gecko can climb smooth surfaces. Their bodies may be very different, but each species is shaped by the same basic challenge: fitting into its world.

*Different Species, Shared Story*

The animal world is full of variety, but beneath the differences are familiar themes. Animals search for food, avoid danger, communicate, care for their young, and find ways to thrive. The more we notice these similarities, the more connected the natural world seems.

# Why the Canucks Need to Be More Mindful of Their Environment

By Naomi

Hockey is played on more than just ice. Every decision the Vancouver Canucks make affects the people, communities, and natural spaces around them. That is why the team should be more mindful of its environment—not only during games, but in every part of its organization.

Mindfulness begins with recognizing the impact of travel, equipment, arena operations, and large sporting events. Reducing unnecessary waste, improving recycling, using energy responsibly, and choosing more sustainable materials can help lessen the team’s environmental footprint. Even small changes, when adopted consistently, can make a meaningful difference.

The Canucks also have an opportunity to inspire their fans. A team with a strong environmental commitment can encourage supporters to use public transportation, avoid single-use plastics, conserve energy, and care for local parks and waterways. Because professional athletes have such a visible platform, their actions can influence thousands of people beyond the rink.

Being mindful of the environment is also about community. Vancouver is surrounded by remarkable natural beauty, and protecting that environment supports the health and well-being of everyone who lives here. By partnering with local organizations, educating young fans, and supporting conservation efforts, the Canucks can show that success is measured not only by wins, but also by the positive legacy a team leaves behind.

The Canucks have the visibility, resources, and influence to lead by example. A more environmentally conscious approach would strengthen their connection with Vancouver and demonstrate that caring for the planet is a responsibility shared by us all.

Naomi thanks you for reading.

To write a good Chinese poem:

1. **Begin with a clear image or emotion**  
   Start from something concrete—rain on a window, a farewell, autumn leaves—rather than an abstract idea.

2. **Use concise, vivid language**  
   Chinese poetry values economy. Choose strong nouns and verbs; remove unnecessary words.

3. **Create rhythm and sound**  
   Pay attention to line length, pauses, repetition, and—especially in classical poetry—rhyme and tonal patterns.

4. **Show emotion indirectly**  
   Let images suggest feelings. “孤灯照旧衣” may express loneliness more powerfully than “我很孤独.”

5. **Build contrast and movement**  
   Pair stillness with motion, light with darkness, past with present, or distance with intimacy.

6. **Use culturally resonant imagery carefully**  
   Moonlight, rivers, plum blossoms, and autumn wind can be powerful, but give familiar images a fresh context.

7. **Revise aloud**  
   Read the poem repeatedly. Replace awkward sounds, cut clichés, and ensure every line contributes something.

A useful structure is:

> **景（scene） → 情（emotion） → 转（shift or insight） → 意（afterthought or resonance）**

For example:

> 雨落空阶晚，  
> 灯明半卷书。  
> 欲寻归去路，  
> 云在故山居。

P.S. A good Chinese poem does not need to sound ancient; clarity, memorable images, and genuine feeling matter most.

The Jesuits came south with books and bells,  
to villages along the Paraná,  
where Guaraní children learned the alphabet  
and old songs learned a new set of words.

They called the settlements reductions—  
not because the people were made small,  
though maps and empires often tried,  
but because lives were gathered  
into towns with plazas, workshops, churches.

“Come see the choir,” someone might say,  
“then stay for the fiesta.”  
Candles climbed the painted walls;  
wooden saints wore bright ribbons;  
the drums argued cheerfully with the organ.

There were gardens, cattle, printing presses,  
a school where a boy could read his own name,  
and a carpenter’s bench warm from the sun.  
There were also orders from faraway kings,  
and borders drawn by men who had never been there.

When Portugal and Spain traded claims,  
the reductions became a question  
on a treaty nobody in the plaza had signed.  
Soldiers arrived. Families moved.  
The church bells kept ringing, but differently.

Still, history is not only collapse.  
Ask the grandmother at the market:  
she remembers a melody, a carved doorway,  
the recipe for festival bread,  
the word fiesta spoken without apology.

The ruins stand in red earth now,  
open to rain, tourists, and birds.  
But listen: beneath the guide’s careful dates,  
someone is still telling the old story—  
not of a vanished people,  
but of what they built,  
and what they refused to forget.

The priest said, “Come in from the forest—  
we’re building a town, not a prison.”  
So Guaraní families came to the Reductions,  
where bells marked dawn,  
fields were measured,  
and the church doors opened onto a new world.

They learned hymns in their own language,  
carved saints with careful hands,  
played violins beneath the red-earth sky.  
At the fiesta, everyone danced—  
though whose customs led the dancing  
was never a simple question.

The Jesuits called it protection  
from slavers and soldiers;  
the empires called it territory.  
Children learned the catechism,  
adults planted maize,  
and the mission ledger counted everything.

Then kings signed papers in distant rooms.  
The Jesuits were expelled.  
The towns were scattered—  
bells silent, workshops empty,  
gardens going wild around the stone.

Still, someone remembers the music.  
Someone sweeps the chapel floor.  
At another fiesta, years later,  
a violin begins again,  
and history sits beside us, saying,  
“Well—what would you have done?”

# Project Proposal: AI for Better Education

## Project Overview

This project will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve education in developing countries. It will support teachers and students through affordable digital tools. The project will focus on local needs. It will also work in areas with limited internet access and few trained teachers.

## Main Goals

- Improve learning outcomes in reading mathematics and science
- Give teachers useful support and training
- Provide lessons that match each student’s learning level
- Expand access to high quality learning materials
- Reduce inequality between urban and rural schools
- Protect student privacy and promote safe technology use

## Key Activities

### 1. Adaptive Learning Platforms

The project will create mobile and web based learning tools. These tools will assess student progress and recommend suitable lessons. Machine learning will identify common errors and provide extra practice.

The system will support local languages and regional curricula. It will also work offline when internet access is limited.

### 2. AI Teaching Assistants

Teachers will receive an AI assistant that can help create lesson plans quizzes and practice activities. It can explain difficult topics and suggest ways to support students who are struggling.

Teachers will remain responsible for all important decisions. The AI will serve as a support tool rather than a replacement for educators.

### 3. Teacher Training

The project will provide training in digital skills teaching methods and responsible AI use. Teachers will learn how to evaluate AI generated content and correct mistakes.

Training will be delivered through workshops mobile courses and peer learning groups.

### 4. Early Warning System

Machine learning will help identify students who may be at risk of falling behind or leaving school. The system may examine attendance assessment results and participation.

Schools will use these signals to offer tutoring counseling or family support. The system will not make final decisions about students.

### 5. Local Learning Content

Local teachers and education experts will help create content that reflects local history culture and daily life. AI tools may assist with translation and adaptation. Human reviewers will check all content for accuracy fairness and cultural respect.

## Implementation Plan

### Phase One: Research and Design

The project team will consult students teachers families and education officials. The team will assess available technology language needs and curriculum goals.

### Phase Two: Pilot Program

The project will launch in a small group of urban and rural schools. Results will be compared with results from similar schools that do not use the system.

### Phase Three: Evaluation

The project will measure reading skills mathematics performance attendance teacher workload and student engagement. It will also collect feedback from families and educators.

### Phase Four: Expansion

After improvements the program will expand through partnerships with ministries of education schools universities nonprofit groups and technology providers.

## Equity and Safety

The project will provide low cost devices where needed. It will support offline access and shared school devices. Special attention will be given to girls students with disabilities rural learners and students from low income families.

Student data will be collected only when necessary. It will be protected through secure storage limited access and clear consent policies. Independent reviewers will test the system for bias and harmful errors.

## Expected Results

- Higher student achievement
- Better support for struggling learners
- More effective lesson planning
- Reduced teacher workload
- Greater access to quality educational materials
- Improved attendance and retention
- Stronger digital skills for students and teachers

## Budget Priorities

Funding will support software development teacher training devices connectivity research evaluation and long term maintenance. A portion of the budget will be reserved for local staff and community partnerships.

## Conclusion

Machine learning and AI can help improve education when they are designed around local needs and guided by teachers. This project will combine technology with human judgment. It will make learning more personal more accessible and more effective for students in developing countries.

Project Summary

The Inclusive Living Lab will investigate practical, affordable ways to improve quality of life for people with disabilities. The project will combine lived experience, accessible technology, community services, and policy research to identify solutions that increase independence, participation, safety, and wellbeing.

Research Questions

  • Which environmental and service barriers most affect daily wellbeing?
  • How can assistive technologies be made more affordable, adaptable, and user-friendly?
  • Which community-based interventions improve social connection and employment access?
  • How can disabled people lead decisions about research, design, and implementation?

Methodology

  1. Participatory design: Establish an advisory board led primarily by people with diverse disabilities.
  2. Needs assessment: Conduct accessible surveys, interviews, home visits, and community workshops.
  3. Prototype development: Co-design solutions such as accessible navigation tools, flexible service models, and personalized support plans.
  4. Pilot evaluation: Test prototypes across urban, rural, and low-income communities for six months.
  5. Impact analysis: Measure independence, mental wellbeing, social participation, service access, and user satisfaction.

Innovation

The project will create an open-access toolkit for local governments, nonprofits, employers, and families. A digital platform, called atlantis, will allow participants to report barriers, share solutions, and track outcomes. A transparent governance framework, known as constable, will document accountability, consent, privacy, and decision-making responsibilities.

Expected Outcomes

  • Evidence-based recommendations for inclusive community planning.
  • Low-cost assistive technology prototypes.
  • Improved access to employment, transportation, healthcare, and social activities.
  • A replicable model for disability-led research.
  • Policy guidance supporting universal design and independent living.

Ethics and Accessibility

All research materials will be available in plain language, large print, captioned video, audio, screen-reader-compatible formats, and relevant communication supports. Participation will be voluntary, compensated, and based on informed consent. Data will be minimized, securely stored, and governed with participants’ direct oversight.

Timeline and Budget

The proposed project will run for 24 months: six months for planning, six months for needs assessment, six months for prototyping, and six months for evaluation and dissemination. Major costs will include participant compensation, accessibility services, research staff, technology development, pilot implementation, and independent evaluation.

Success Criteria

Success will be defined by measurable improvements in participant-reported quality of life, successful adoption of tested solutions, reduced barriers to essential services, and continued use of the toolkit by community organizations after the project ends.

# Project Proposal: AI for Better Education

## Project Summary

This project will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve education in developing countries. It will support teachers and students through affordable digital tools that work in local languages and with limited internet access.

## Main Goals

- Improve access to high quality learning materials
- Personalize lessons for each student
- Support teachers with planning and assessment
- Identify learning gaps at an early stage
- Expand education in rural and underserved communities

## Proposed Activities

### 1. Adaptive Learning Platform

We will develop a mobile platform that adjusts lessons according to each student’s progress. The system will recommend suitable exercises and provide immediate feedback.

### 2. AI Teacher Assistant

An AI assistant will help teachers create lesson plans and quizzes. It will also suggest teaching strategies and summarize student performance.

### 3. Local Language Content

Machine learning tools will translate and adapt learning materials into local languages. Content will reflect local culture and community needs.

### 4. Offline Access

The platform will function on basic smartphones and low cost computers. Lessons will be available offline and will synchronize when internet access returns.

### 5. Early Support System

The system will analyze learning activity to identify students who may need additional help. Teachers and school leaders will receive clear recommendations.

## Implementation Plan

The project will begin with a pilot in selected schools. Local teachers and education officials will help design and test the tools. After evaluation the program will expand to more schools and regions.

Training will be provided for teachers school leaders and technical staff. Community workshops will explain the benefits and limits of AI.

## Safeguards

Student data will be protected through strong security measures. The project will collect only necessary information and will follow local privacy laws. Teachers will remain responsible for important decisions. AI will support human judgment rather than replace it.

## Expected Results

- Higher student engagement
- Better reading and mathematics outcomes
- Reduced teacher workload
- Faster identification of learning difficulties
- Wider access to quality education
- Stronger use of local languages in schools

## Evaluation

Success will be measured through student assessments teacher surveys attendance records and platform usage. Results will be compared with conditions before the pilot. Independent reviewers will assess educational impact equity cost and safety.

## Budget Priorities

Funding will support software development teacher training local content creation device access research and long term maintenance. Partnerships with governments universities nonprofit groups and technology organizations will help reduce costs.

## Conclusion

Responsible use of AI can help developing countries provide more inclusive and effective education. By combining local leadership with affordable technology this project will give students better learning opportunities and help teachers serve their communities.

写好一首中文诗，可以从以下方面入手：

1. **先确定核心情感**  
   想清楚你要表达的是思念、喜悦、孤独、愤怒，还是对自然与人生的感悟。情感越明确，诗越有力量。

2. **用具体意象代替抽象表达**  
   少说“我很悲伤”，多写“雨打空阶，灯影渐凉”。月、江、雁、旧衣、黄昏等意象，能让情绪变得可感。

3. **锤炼语言与节奏**  
   中文诗重视音韵、停顿和朗读感。删去多余字词，尝试不同句式，让每一行都有呼吸和力度。

4. **创造新鲜的比喻**  
   避免陈词滥调，寻找属于自己的联想。例如，不写“时间像流水”，而写“旧钟把黄昏一格格推远”。

5. **讲究留白**  
   不必把意思全部解释清楚。适当含蓄，让读者参与补全情绪，诗会更有余味。

6. **让意象彼此关联**  
   一首诗中的景物最好围绕同一情绪或主题展开，避免意象堆砌。

7. **反复修改并朗读**  
   写完后大声读几遍，检查是否顺口、是否有突兀之处，并大胆删改。

一个简单的写作步骤是：**确定情感 → 选择场景 → 捕捉意象 → 组织节奏 → 留下余韵**。

**P.S.** 好诗不一定复杂，关键是用准确而独特的语言，说出真实的感受。

# What Animals Have in Common

*We all need a little energy*

From tiny ants to giant elephants, animals spend a lot of time looking for food, water, and safe places to rest. Their menus may be completely different, but the basic goal is the same: get enough energy to survive the day.

*Family matters*

Many animals care for their young. Birds build nests, wolves raise pups together, and whales stay close to their calves. Even when parenting looks different, the idea is familiar: protect the babies, teach them important skills, and help them grow up.

*Communication is everywhere*

Animals may not use human language, but they are constantly sending messages. Dogs bark, bees dance, dolphins whistle, and wolves howl. Body posture, color, scent, and movement can also say, “Stay away,” “Come here,” or “There’s food nearby.”

*Everyone wants to feel safe*

Nearly every species has ways to avoid danger. Some run, some hide, and some fight back. A turtle has its shell, a skunk has its smell, and a stick insect has camouflage. These strategies differ, but they all solve the same problem: staying alive.

*Friendship and teamwork help*

Animals often cooperate because working together makes life easier. Meerkats take turns watching for predators, dolphins may hunt as a group, and chimpanzees groom one another. Social bonds can provide protection, food, comfort, and companionship.

*Play is more important than it looks*

Young animals wrestle, chase, pounce, and practice hunting. Otters slide down muddy banks, fox kits tumble around, and crows play with objects. Play is fun, but it also helps animals learn, build strength, and understand their surroundings.

*Adaptation keeps life moving*

Animals are wonderfully creative when it comes to fitting into their environments. Camels conserve water, penguins stay warm in icy climates, and desert rodents are active at night. Species may look and behave very differently, yet each is responding to the same challenge: how to thrive where it lives.

In the end, animals are more alike than they first appear. Beneath feathers, fur, scales, and shells, they are all trying to eat, communicate, stay safe, care for others, and make their way through the world.

When you look at a dog, a dolphin, and a bird, they might seem completely different. One barks, one swims, and one flies. But underneath those obvious differences, animals share many surprising traits.

*Everyone Needs a Home*

Almost every animal needs a safe place to rest, raise young, and escape danger. Birds build nests, rabbits dig burrows, and elephants travel together for protection. Even tiny insects carefully choose places to live and reproduce.

*Communication Is Everywhere*

Animals are constantly sending messages. Wolves howl, bees dance, whales sing, and meerkats make alarm calls. Body language matters too—cats arch their backs, dogs wag their tails, and gorillas beat their chests. In their own ways, animals are always saying, “Pay attention!”

*Families Stick Together*

Many species care deeply for their young. Bears teach cubs how to find food, penguins take turns protecting eggs, and elephants help raise calves as a group. Parental care looks different from species to species, but the basic idea is familiar: young animals need guidance and protection.

*Play Isn’t Just for Humans*

Young animals love to play, but adults do it too. Otters slide down muddy banks, monkeys chase each other, and dolphins leap through waves. Play helps animals practice important skills, build relationships, and simply enjoy themselves.

*Animals Solve Problems*

Animals can be clever problem-solvers. Crows use tools, octopuses open containers, and chimpanzees remember complicated routes to find food. Even squirrels adapt their hiding spots when other animals are watching. Intelligence comes in many forms.

*Rest and Relaxation Matter*

All animals need downtime. Cats nap in sunny windows, bats sleep upside down, and whales take short rests while swimming. Rest helps animals recover energy and stay alert—something humans can definitely relate to.

The animal world is full of differences, but those differences often hide familiar patterns. Whether an animal has feathers, fur, scales, or fins, it still needs food, safety, communication, companionship, and rest. The more we learn about other species, the more connected life on Earth seems.

"Let \(x\) be the number of members with 3 pets.

To maximize \(x\), the other 20 − \(x\) members each have exactly 1 pet.

Total pets: \(3x + (20 - x) = 32\)

\(2x + 20 = 32\)

\(2x = 12\)

\(x = 6\)

Therefore, the maximum number of members who can have 3 pets is \(\boxed{6}\)."

# Project Proposal: ai-powered education for developing countries

## purpose

This project will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve access to effective education in developing countries. It will support teachers and provide students with personalized learning that works in local languages and low-resource settings.

## objectives

- improve student learning outcomes
- expand access to quality educational content
- support teachers with practical tools
- identify learning gaps at an early stage
- reduce inequality between urban and rural schools

## project design

The project will create an offline-first learning platform for schools and community centers. Students will use affordable smartphones tablets or shared computers to access lessons quizzes and practice activities.

Machine learning systems will analyze student responses and identify areas of strength and difficulty. The platform will then recommend suitable exercises and explanations. Content will be adapted to each student’s level and learning pace.

An ai tutor will provide guided support in local languages. It will answer common questions explain difficult ideas and encourage students to seek help from teachers when needed. The system will not replace teachers. It will help them spend more time on instruction mentoring and individual support.

Teachers will receive dashboards that show class progress and common learning gaps. They will receive suggestions for lessons activities and targeted support. Teacher training will cover digital skills responsible ai use and the interpretation of learning data.

## local partnership

The project will work with ministries of education local schools universities teachers and community organizations. Local educators will help create and review content. Linguists and cultural experts will ensure that lessons are accurate respectful and relevant.

## technology and access

The platform will function with limited internet access. Content will be stored on local devices or school servers and updated when a connection is available. The system will use open standards and affordable hardware. Solar charging options will be considered for schools with unreliable electricity.

## safety and fairness

Student data will be protected through strong security and clear consent procedures. The project will collect only necessary information. Human review will be required for important decisions about student placement or support.

Models will be tested for bias across languages regions genders and income groups. Families and teachers will receive clear explanations of how the system works. Students will always have access to human assistance.

## implementation

### phase one

Select pilot regions and assess local needs. Build the platform and create curriculum aligned content in several local languages.

### phase two

Launch pilots in selected schools. Train teachers and gather feedback from students families and education leaders.

### phase three

Measure learning outcomes improve the system and expand to additional regions.

## evaluation

Success will be measured through:

- gains in reading mathematics and science
- student attendance and engagement
- teacher satisfaction and time saved
- access for rural and underserved learners
- quality of local language content
- responsible use of student data

## expected impact

The project will help more students receive timely support and high quality learning opportunities. It will strengthen teachers rather than displace them. With careful governance and local leadership it can create a scalable model for more inclusive and effective education.

写好一首中文诗，可以从以下方面入手：

1. **先确定核心感受**  
   不要一开始就追求华丽辞藻，先明确你想表达的是思念、孤独、喜悦，还是对某件事的感悟。

2. **用具体意象代替抽象说明**  
   少说“我很悲伤”，多写“雨停在半开的窗上”。月亮、旧信、车站、秋风等具体事物，能让情感更鲜明。

3. **锤炼语言**  
   诗歌讲究简洁。删去可有可无的词，选择准确、有画面感和声音感的字词。

4. **重视节奏与分行**  
   中文诗的节奏来自字数、停顿、重复和分行。朗读诗句，听它是否自然、有起伏。

5. **建立意象之间的联系**  
   不要堆砌漂亮意象。让景物共同服务于主题，形成内在的情绪线索。

6. **适当使用比喻和拟人**  
   比如：“黄昏把影子拉得很长。”好的修辞应当让感受更深，而不是显得炫技。

7. **保留含蓄与余韵**  
   不必把意思全部说尽。给读者留下想象空间，诗才更耐读。

8. **反复修改**  
   写完后隔一段时间再读，检查是否空泛、重复或矫饰。尝试删掉一半，往往能让诗更有力量。

一个简单的写作练习是：选择一个普通物件，如“钥匙”，写出它的颜色、声音、触感，再联想到一个记忆，最后用一句未完全说尽的话收尾。

**P.S.** 好诗不一定复杂，真诚、准确、耐读，往往比华丽更重要。

# The Canucks and the Power of Environmental Awareness

By Naomi

Success in hockey depends on more than skill, speed, and determination. It also depends on awareness—knowing where teammates are, reading the ice, anticipating opponents, and responding to changing conditions. That same mindset should extend beyond the rink. The Vancouver Canucks have an opportunity to become more mindful of the environments they influence every day.

As a professional sports organization, the Canucks reach millions of people. Their choices—from travel and energy use to waste management and community partnerships—can have a meaningful impact. By reducing unnecessary waste, improving recycling and composting, conserving energy, and supporting sustainable transportation, the team can demonstrate that environmental responsibility belongs in every part of modern sports.

Mindfulness also means considering the broader community. The Canucks play in a region surrounded by forests, mountains, waterways, and diverse neighborhoods. Protecting these spaces helps preserve the quality of life that makes British Columbia special. Supporting local environmental programs, educating fans, and working with community organizations could turn the team’s visibility into positive action.

Fans, too, are influenced by what their team values. When players and leaders model thoughtful habits, supporters may be encouraged to make better choices at home, at work, and while attending games. Small actions—bringing reusable items, using public transit, avoiding litter, and respecting shared spaces—can become part of a larger culture of care.

Being mindful of the environment is not a distraction from competition. It is another form of preparation, discipline, and leadership. The Canucks have the platform to show that excellence includes responsibility—not only for what happens on the ice, but also for the world beyond it.

Naomi thanks you for reading.

# Why the Canucks Need to Be More Mindful of Their Environment

By Naomi

Hockey is played in a fast-moving environment where every detail matters. For the Canucks, being mindful of their surroundings can make the difference between reacting too late and creating the next great opportunity.

Environmental awareness means more than noticing where the puck is. It means understanding the positioning of teammates, recognizing defensive pressure, reading changes in momentum, and anticipating what may happen before it does. The best players do not simply respond to the game—they see it developing.

This awareness begins on the ice. Players must communicate consistently, maintain strong spacing, and remain alert even when they are away from the puck. A moment of lost focus can create an open lane, a missed assignment, or an unnecessary penalty. By staying engaged with the entire rink, the Canucks can make smarter decisions and support one another more effectively.

Mindfulness also applies beyond the game. The team’s environment includes the locker room, coaching staff, fans, travel schedule, and the expectations surrounding a proud franchise. A positive and focused team culture can help players stay resilient during difficult stretches. Listening carefully, respecting different perspectives, and responding thoughtfully can strengthen trust throughout the organization.

The Canucks also have an opportunity to be mindful of their broader community and physical surroundings. As a visible Vancouver team, they can model responsibility by supporting local initiatives, reducing waste, and encouraging sustainable habits among fans. Leadership is not limited to what happens during the sixty minutes of a game.

When the Canucks become more attentive to their environments, they gain a clearer understanding of both challenges and opportunities. Greater awareness can improve communication, sharpen reactions, strengthen teamwork, and help the team remain composed under pressure.

The game rewards those who see more than what is immediately in front of them. For the Canucks, mindfulness can be a competitive advantage—and a meaningful way to grow as athletes, teammates, and community leaders.

Naomi thanks you for reading.

# Animal Species Are More Alike Than We Think

Animals can look wildly different, but beneath the feathers, fur, scales, and shells, many of them have surprisingly similar lives.

*They all need food and water*

From tiny ants to giant elephants, every animal needs energy to survive. Some hunt, some graze, and others filter food from the water, but the goal is the same: find nutrients and stay healthy.

*Family matters*

Many animals care for their young, even if they do it in different ways. Birds build nests, wolves raise pups in packs, and whales protect their calves while swimming through the ocean. Parenting may look different, but keeping babies safe is a common theme.

*Communication is everywhere*

Animals are constantly sending messages. Dogs bark, dolphins whistle, bees dance, and elephants use low rumbles that can travel long distances. These signals help animals warn each other, find mates, claim territory, or simply stay connected.

*Everyone needs a safe place*

Animals look for shelter from weather and predators. A rabbit might hide in a burrow, a bird may settle into a tree, and a crab can retreat into its shell. Even animals that migrate or roam widely still need secure places to rest.

*Play is not just for humans*

Young animals often play by chasing, wrestling, climbing, or practicing hunting skills. Otters slide down muddy banks, fox kits pounce on one another, and young monkeys swing through trees. Play helps them learn, build strength, and form friendships.

*They adapt to challenges*

Animals are excellent problem-solvers. Camels conserve water in hot deserts, polar bears rely on thick fur and body fat, and octopuses change color to hide. Each species has its own toolkit for handling the world around it.

*We share more than we realize*

The biggest similarity across animal species is that they are all trying to survive and thrive in their own environments. Their bodies may be completely different, but their basic needs—food, safety, connection, and care—are remarkably familiar. Looking at animals this way makes the natural world feel less distant and a lot more relatable.

# Why the Canucks Need to Be More Mindful of Their Environment

By Naomi

For the Vancouver Canucks, success depends on more than skill, effort, and strategy. It also depends on awareness—awareness of the environments in which players practice, compete, recover, and connect with fans. A team that pays close attention to its surroundings can make smarter decisions, build stronger relationships, and perform with greater consistency.

Being mindful of the environment means recognizing how physical spaces affect the team. Clean, well-maintained facilities support health, focus, and recovery. Thoughtful travel routines, responsible energy use, and reduced waste can help create a more sustainable organization. Even small choices, such as reusing equipment when possible or limiting unnecessary consumption, can contribute to a larger positive impact.

Environmental mindfulness also extends beyond the rink. The Canucks represent Vancouver, a city known for its natural beauty and strong community spirit. As a prominent organization, the team has an opportunity to model responsible behavior for supporters throughout British Columbia. Supporting local initiatives, reducing the environmental impact of events, and encouraging fans to make sustainable choices can turn the team’s influence into meaningful action.

The social environment matters just as much. Players perform best when they feel respected, supported, and heard. Coaches, executives, teammates, and staff all help shape a culture where accountability and empathy are valued. Paying attention to team dynamics can prevent small tensions from becoming larger problems and can create the trust necessary for players to work together under pressure.

Mindfulness also means understanding the atmosphere surrounding each game. Fans bring passion and energy, but that energy should be guided by respect—for opponents, officials, staff, and one another. The Canucks can help establish a positive standard by promoting inclusion, sportsmanship, and community responsibility.

Ultimately, being mindful of the environment is not a distraction from hockey. It is part of building a stronger team. When the Canucks take care of their facilities, community, culture, and natural surroundings, they create the conditions for long-term success both on and off the ice.

Naomi thanks you for reading.

We started with a map, a mission, a river—  
not heaven exactly, but a place to begin.  
The Jesuits called them *reductions*:  
towns gathered from the forest,  
Guaraní families learning prayers  
beside bells cast from melted tools.

“Come in,” the priests said, “bring your language,  
your songs, your way of planting maize.”  
And still, they measured streets,  
built churches with painted saints,  
taught the children Latin in the morning  
and music—vio­lins, flutes—after rain.

There was a fiesta on Saint Ignatius’ day,  
red cloth in the square, cassava on the table,  
a choir singing so beautifully  
that even the governor stopped talking.  
Another fiesta came at harvest,  
with dancing late and candles floating  
like small boats before the altar.

But let’s be honest:  
a reduction could mean protection  
from slave hunters—and control  
by men who arrived with crosses,  
maps, and orders from far away.  
The village had its own council,  
yet someone else had drawn the boundaries.

Then empires changed their coats.  
Spain and Portugal argued over rivers,  
and soldiers came with paperwork and guns.  
The missions were closed,  
the bells went quiet,  
and families carried their memories  
back through the grass.

Still, the old songs stayed.  
So did the stories:  
of a church built by many hands,  
of a fiesta that lasted until dawn,  
of a place reduced on paper  
but never reduced in the heart.

# Why the Canucks Need to Be More Mindful of Their Environment

By Naomi

For the Vancouver Canucks, success depends on more than talent, strategy, and determination. It also depends on awareness—of the ice, the arena, the community, and the world around them.

Environmental mindfulness also matters beyond the rink. The Canucks have a powerful influence on Vancouver and their fans. By reducing waste, conserving energy, supporting sustainable transportation, and encouraging responsible habits, they can help protect the beautiful region they represent.

The team can also lead by example through community partnerships, environmental education, and initiatives that connect hockey with local conservation. These efforts would show young fans that caring for nature and caring for one another are part of being a strong teammate.

Mindfulness is not a distraction from competition. It is a competitive advantage. When the Canucks understand their surroundings, respect their community, and recognize their broader impact, they become more thoughtful athletes and more meaningful representatives of Vancouver.

# What Animals Have in Common

Animals may look wildly different, but many species share surprisingly similar habits, skills, and emotions.

*1. Family Matters*

From elephants and wolves to penguins and humans, many animals form strong family groups. Parents protect, teach, and sometimes even play with their young. Baby animals may depend on adults for years while learning how to find food and stay safe.

*2. Communication Is Everywhere*

Animals communicate in all kinds of ways. Birds sing, dolphins whistle, dogs bark, and bees dance to show where food is. Even body language—like wagging a tail, puffing up feathers, or showing teeth—can send a clear message.

*3. Everyone Needs a Home*

Whether it’s a bird’s nest, a beaver’s dam, a fox’s den, or a human house, animals create or choose places that offer safety and comfort. These homes help protect them from weather, predators, and danger.

*4. Play Isn’t Just for Fun*

Young mammals chase each other, ravens slide down snowy roofs, and octopuses explore objects for amusement. Play helps animals practice important skills, build relationships, and learn about their surroundings.

*5. Teamwork Makes Life Easier*

Ants build colonies, wolves hunt in packs, dolphins cooperate to catch fish, and monkeys warn one another about predators. Working together often helps animals find food, defend themselves, and care for their group.

*6. Animals Adapt to Change*

Species across the planet have developed clever ways to survive. Camels store energy for desert journeys, polar bears have thick fur, and birds migrate when the seasons change. Adaptation allows animals to live in environments that seem almost impossible.

The more we study animals, the more familiar they seem. Underneath all the differences in size, shape, and habitat, many species share the same basic needs: food, safety, companionship, and a chance to thrive.

*Animals Are More Alike Than We Think*

When you look at a dog, an elephant, and a tiny ant, they seem completely different. But beneath the fur, feathers, scales, and shells, many animals share surprisingly similar habits and needs.

*1. Everyone Needs Food and Energy*

All animals need energy to survive. Whether it’s a lion hunting, a hummingbird sipping nectar, or a cow munching grass, every species has developed its own way to find and use food. Even animals that eat very different things often share similar strategies, such as searching, storing, or competing for meals.

*2. Communication Is Everywhere*

Animals communicate constantly. Wolves howl, birds sing, bees dance, and dolphins click. These signals can warn others about danger, attract mates, defend territory, or simply help a group stay together. Humans use words, but animals have plenty of conversations of their own.

*3. Families Matter*

Many animals care for their young, sometimes for years. Birds build nests and feed their chicks, elephants protect calves, and primates teach babies how to find food. Even species that live alone often spend important time raising and protecting their offspring.

*4. Animals Play and Learn*

Play isn’t just for pets. Young mammals wrestle, birds practice flying, and some octopuses investigate objects for fun. Play helps animals develop skills, explore their surroundings, and prepare for adult life. It may even be a way to build friendships.

*5. Cooperation Helps Everyone*

Animals often work together. Ants form organized colonies, meerkats take turns watching for predators, and fish swim in groups for protection. Cooperation can make finding food, raising young, and avoiding danger much easier.

*6. Rest Is Essential*

Every animal needs downtime. Cats nap, bats sleep upside down, and migrating birds take breaks during long journeys. Rest allows bodies to recover and brains to process information. Even the busiest creatures need a little quiet time.

*7. Adaptation Connects Us All*

Animals have adapted to survive in nearly every environment on Earth. Camels store energy for desert journeys, penguins stay warm in icy waters, and tree frogs use sticky toes to climb. Their bodies may look different, but the basic goal is the same: find a way to live successfully.

The animal kingdom is full of variety, but those differences can hide some familiar patterns. Food, family, communication, play, teamwork, and rest are threads connecting species across the planet—including us.

"score": 1, "feedback": "{\"answer\": \"\\n\\n\\n \\n \\n Inclusive Living Research Project Proposal\\n\\n\\n
\\n

Project Proposal: Pathways to Inclusive Living

\\n\\n
\\n

Overview

\\n

\\n This research project will identify practical, scalable ways to improve quality of life\\n for people with disabilities by combining lived experience, accessible technology,\\n community services, and policy innovation.\\n

\\n
\\n\\n
\\n

Research Questions

\\n
    \\n
  • Which barriers most significantly affect independence, health, employment, and social connection?
    • \\n
  • Which assistive technologies and community interventions produce measurable benefits?
    • \\n
  • How can public services be designed with disabled people rather than merely for them?
    • \\n
\\n
\\n\\n
\\n

Methods

\\n
    \\n
  1. Conduct participatory workshops and interviews with people across disability communities.
    2. \\n
  2. Map barriers in housing, transportation, healthcare, education, and employment.
    3. \\n
  3. Co-design and pilot interventions with local organizations and service providers.
    4. \\n
  4. Evaluate outcomes using measures of autonomy, wellbeing, accessibility, participation, and cost.
    5. \\n
\\n
\\n\\n
\\n

Innovation

\\n

\\n The project will create an open-access \\u201cInclusive Living Toolkit\\u201d containing tested\\n design standards, service models, policy recommendations, and implementation guidance.\\n A demonstration program, called Atlantis, will test how integrated\\n digital and in-person support can help people navigate services independently.\\n The evaluation framework, Constable, will track outcomes over time while\\n protecting privacy and participant control.\\n

\\n
\\n\\n
\\n

Expected Impact

\\n
    \\n
  • Improved independence and daily wellbeing.
    • \\n
  • More accessible public services and workplaces.
    • \\n
  • Evidence-based recommendations for policymakers.
    • \\n
  • Transferable tools for disability organizations and communities.
    • \\n
\\n
\\n\\n
\\n

Ethics and Inclusion

\\n

\\n Disabled people will be paid as research partners, represented in governance, and involved\\n in every stage of the project. Materials and participation options will be accessible,\\n data will be minimized and securely stored, and findings will be shared in plain-language,\\n audio, captioned, and screen-reader-friendly formats.\\n

\\n
\\n\\n
\\n

Timeline

\\n

\\n The proposed project will run for 24 months: six months for community consultation,\\n six months for co-design, eight months for pilot testing, and four months for analysis\\n and dissemination.\\n

\\n

写好一首中文诗，可以从这几步开始：

1. **先确定核心情感**  
   选择一个具体感受，如思念、孤独、喜悦或惆怅，不要一开始就追求华丽辞藻。

2. **用具体意象表达**  
   少直接说“我很悲伤”，多写“雨停后，窗台还留着你的影子”。月、风、灯、河流等意象，要服务于情绪。

3. **注意语言的凝练**  
   删除多余的字，让每一句都有重量。中文诗尤其讲究节奏、停顿和声音的回响。

4. **制造画面与转折**  
   让诗中出现变化：由远及近、由明转暗、由回忆回到现实。转折往往能提升诗的张力。

5. **保留含蓄与余味**  
   不必把意思全部解释清楚，给读者留下想象空间。

6. **反复修改并朗读**  
   读出声，检查是否顺口、是否有重复、是否过于抽象。好诗通常是改出来的。

> 一个场景 + 一个细节 + 一种情感 + 一个余韵

> 黄昏落在旧站台，  
> 风替我翻动空白的车票。  
> 远处列车亮起灯，  
> 像你没有说完的话。

P.S. 写诗时，真诚通常比华丽更重要。

# The Canucks and the Power of a Mindful Environment

By Naomi

Success in hockey depends on more than skill, speed, and strategy. The environment surrounding a team can shape how players think, communicate, recover, and perform. For the Vancouver Canucks, becoming more mindful of their environments could create meaningful advantages both on and off the ice.

A team’s environment includes its locker room, training facilities, travel routines, coaching culture, fan atmosphere, and online presence. Each of these spaces affects confidence and focus. A supportive environment can help players feel prepared and connected, while a stressful or distracting one can make it harder to stay composed during challenging moments.

Mindfulness begins with awareness. Players and staff can pay closer attention to how noise, lighting, schedules, relationships, and expectations influence their energy and concentration. Small adjustments—such as creating quiet recovery spaces, encouraging open communication, and protecting time for rest—can support better physical and mental performance.

The Canucks can also benefit from building an environment where accountability and compassion work together. High standards matter, but so does recognizing that every player faces pressure differently. When teammates feel respected and heard, they are more likely to communicate honestly, learn from mistakes, and support one another through difficult stretches.

The team’s connection with Vancouver matters as well. The city, its fans, and the wider hockey community contribute to the atmosphere around the club. By engaging thoughtfully with supporters and representing the community with care, the Canucks can strengthen a shared sense of purpose.

Being mindful of the environment does not mean avoiding pressure or discomfort. It means understanding how surroundings affect performance and deliberately shaping those surroundings to help people thrive. For a team pursuing lasting success, awareness can become a competitive strength.

Naomi thanks you for reading.

# Project Proposal: AI for Better Education

## Project Overview

This project will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve education in developing countries. The program will support teachers and students through affordable digital tools that work in local languages and in areas with limited internet access.

## Goals

- Improve access to quality learning materials
- Support teachers with useful classroom tools
- Provide learning support based on student needs
- Reduce gaps between urban and rural schools
- Strengthen skills in reading mathematics and science
- Promote safe fair and inclusive use of AI

## Main Activities

### 1. AI Learning Platform

We will create a mobile friendly learning platform with lessons quizzes and practice exercises. The platform will adjust content according to each student’s progress. It will provide easier or more advanced activities when needed.

The system will support local languages and allow students to download lessons for offline use.

### 2. Teacher Support Tools

AI tools will help teachers prepare lessons create exercises and identify common learning problems. Teachers will remain responsible for all important decisions. The tools will offer suggestions rather than replace educators.

Training will help teachers use the system with confidence.

### 3. Local Learning Content

Local educators will work with technology experts to create content that reflects local culture history and community needs. The project will include materials for students with disabilities.

### 4. Early Warning Support

Machine learning will identify signs that a student may be falling behind or leaving school. Teachers and community workers can then provide support such as tutoring mentoring or financial assistance.

### 5. Teacher Training

The project will provide practical training in digital education AI literacy privacy and responsible technology use. Teacher communities will allow educators to share ideas and successful practices.

## Implementation Plan

### Phase One: Research and Design

We will consult students teachers families education leaders and local organizations. These discussions will identify priorities language needs infrastructure limits and cultural concerns.

### Phase Two: Pilot Program

The project will launch in a small group of urban rural and remote schools. We will test the platform with teachers and students and improve it using their feedback.

### Phase Three: Expansion

After reviewing the pilot results we will expand the program through partnerships with ministries of education schools universities nonprofit groups and telecommunications providers.

## Infrastructure

The system will be designed for low cost devices and slow networks. It will support offline access through local servers memory cards and downloadable lessons. Solar powered equipment may be used in schools with unreliable electricity.

## Privacy and Safety

Student data will be collected only when necessary. Personal information will be protected through strong security measures. Families and schools will receive clear information about data use.

AI systems will be tested for bias and accuracy. Human review will be required for decisions that affect student opportunities.

## Evaluation

Success will be measured through:

- Improvement in reading mathematics and science
- Student attendance and engagement
- Teacher confidence and workload
- Use of learning materials
- Progress among rural students and disadvantaged groups
- Cost per student
- Retention in school

Independent researchers will review results and publish findings.

## Expected Results

The project will help students learn at their own pace and give teachers better information about student needs. It will increase access to quality education and support communities that lack trained educators or learning resources.

## Budget Priorities

Funding will support software development teacher training local content creation devices connectivity research and long term maintenance. Partnerships will reduce costs and help schools continue the program after initial funding ends.

## Conclusion

AI can improve education when it is affordable locally relevant and guided by teachers. This project will combine machine learning with human support to create stronger learning opportunities for students in developing countries.

# Interesting Facts About the Dutch Language

Dutch is spoken by more than 20 million people, mainly in the Netherlands and Belgium, where it is known as Dutch and Flemish respectively. It is also an official language in Suriname and several Caribbean islands.

## A Language Between English and German

Dutch belongs to the West Germanic language family, alongside English and German. As a result, many Dutch words resemble English words:

- *water* — water  
- *boek* — book  
- *appel* — apple  
- *hand* — hand  

Dutch grammar and pronunciation also share features with German, although Dutch is generally considered somewhat simpler to learn.

## *Dutch Has Some Remarkably Long Words*

Dutch commonly combines several words into one. For example, *kindercarnavalsoptochtvoorbereidingswerkzaamhedenplan* refers to a plan for preparing children’s carnival parade activities. Such words may look intimidating, but their meaning can usually be understood by breaking them into smaller parts.

## *The “G” Sound Is Famous*

One of the most recognizable features of Dutch pronunciation is the hard, throaty “g” sound, especially in the northern Netherlands. It is produced at the back of the throat and can take practice for learners. In southern Dutch varieties, including many forms of Flemish, this sound is often softer.

## Dutch Has Two Words for “You”

Dutch uses *jij* or *je* for informal situations and *u* for formal ones. The choice depends on age, familiarity, and social setting. In modern everyday speech, informal forms are increasingly common, but *u* remains important in professional and respectful communication.

## It Has Three Grammatical Articles

Dutch nouns use the articles *de*, *het*, and *een*. Both *de* and *het* mean “the,” while *een* means “a” or “an.” Unfortunately for learners, whether a noun takes *de* or *het* often must be memorized, although diminutive nouns ending in *-je* always use *het*.

## Dutch Influenced Other Languages

Dutch sailors, traders, and settlers carried words around the world. English words such as *cookie*, *yacht*, *freight*, *landscape*, and *boss* have Dutch origins. Indonesian, Afrikaans, and several Caribbean languages have also been strongly influenced by Dutch.

## Afrikaans Grew from Dutch

Afrikaans developed largely from seventeenth-century Dutch spoken in southern Africa. The two languages remain closely related, but Afrikaans has simpler grammar and different vocabulary. A Dutch speaker can often recognize written Afrikaans, even when the meaning is not immediately clear.

## “Dutch” Does Not Mean “From Germany”

The English word “Dutch” once referred more broadly to Germanic-speaking people. Over time, its meaning narrowed in English to describe the Netherlands and its language. This is why “Dutch” and “Deutsch,” the German word for German, look and sound related.

Dutch combines familiar vocabulary, distinctive sounds, flexible word formation, and a rich international history. That mixture makes it an especially fascinating language to explore.
